The proposition of prediction, the proposition of non-prediction. The proposition of the icchantika, the proposition of non-icchantika. The proposition of women, men, and neither, the proposition of no women, men, and neither. The proposition of taste, the proposition of non-taste. The proposition of things, the proposition of non-things. The proposition of the body, the proposition of non-body. The proposition of enlightenment, the proposition of non-enlightenment. The proposition of movement, the proposition of non-movement. The proposition of the faculties, the proposition of non-faculties. The proposition of the conditioned, the proposition of the unconditioned. The proposition of the unconditioned, the proposition of non-unconditioned. The proposition of cause and fruit, the proposition of no cause and fruit. The proposition of the utmost limit of form, the proposition of no utmost limit of form. The proposition of the joints, the proposition of non-joints. The proposition of the dense trees and vines, the proposition of no dense trees and vines. The proposition of the mixed, the proposition of non-mixed. The proposition of teaching, the proposition of non-teaching. The proposition of the Vinaya, the proposition of non-Vinaya. The proposition of monks, the proposition of non-monks. The proposition of the sense-fields, the proposition of non-sense-fields. The proposition of letters, the proposition of non-letters. Mahamati! These hundred and eight propositions were spoken by the Buddhas of the past; you and the bodhisattva-mahasattvas should study them.”
Then the great bodhisattva Mahamati again addressed the Buddha, saying: ‘World-honored One, how many kinds of arising, dwelling, and ceasing are there among the consciousnesses?’

The Buddha told Mahamati: ‘The consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, dwelling, and ceasing, which cannot be known by reasoning. They have two kinds of arising: the arising of the continuous stream and the arising of the characteristics. They have two kinds of dwelling: the dwelling of the continuous stream and the dwelling of the characteristics. They have two kinds of ceasing: the ceasing of the continuous stream and the ceasing of the characteristics. The consciousnesses have three kinds of characteristics: the characteristic of transformation, the characteristic of karma, and the characteristic of reality. Mahamati! Briefly stated, there are three kinds of consciousnesses; spoken of in full, there are eight. What are the three? The true consciousness, the manifesting consciousness, and the consciousness that discriminates particular objects. Mahamati! It is like a bright mirror which holds up all forms; the manifesting consciousness likewise reveals itself in its own place. Mahamati! The manifesting consciousness and the consciousness that discriminates particular objects — these two, in their mutual destructibility and indestructibility, are the causes that turn one upon the other. Mahamati! Inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation are the cause of the manifesting consciousness. Mahamati! The grasping of the various sense-objects and the perfuming of beginningless deluded thought are the cause of the consciousness that discriminates particular objects. Mahamati! If one turns back that true consciousness, and the various unreal and false notions cease, then all the consciousnesses of the sense-organs cease. Mahamati! This is called the ceasing of the characteristics. Mahamati! As for the ceasing of the continuous stream: when the cause of the continuous stream ceases, then the continuous stream ceases; when that from which it arises ceases and that upon which it depends ceases, then the continuous stream ceases. Mahamati! Why is this so? Because it is that upon which they depend. The dependence is called the perfuming of beginningless deluded thought. The occasion refers to the consciousness-fields and the deluded views of self-mind, such as the seeing of one’s own mind. Mahamati! It is like a lump of clay and the dust-particles: neither different nor not different. Likewise with gold and the ornament made from it. Mahamati! If a lump of clay and its dust-particles were different, then the lump would not be made of them; but in fact it is made of them, and so they are not different. If they were not different, then the lump of clay and the dust-particles would be without distinction. So too, Mahamati! If the transforming consciousness, the store consciousness, and the true characteristic were different from one another, the store consciousness would not be their cause; but if they were not different, then when the transforming consciousness ceased, the store consciousness should also cease. Yet the true characteristic in reality does not cease. Therefore, Mahamati! It is not the true characteristic consciousness that ceases, but only the characteristic of karma that ceases. If the true characteristic ceased, then the store consciousness would cease. Mahamati! If the store consciousness ceased, it would be no different from the nihilistic arguments of the externalists. Mahamati! Those externalists argue thus: ‘When the realm of grasping ceases, the stream of the consciousnesses also ceases. If the stream of the consciousnesses ceases, then the beginningless stream should be cut off.’ Mahamati! The externalists speak of a cause for the arising of the stream that is not the coming together of the eye-consciousness, forms, and light, but some other cause. Mahamati! That cause they declare to be: whether the Supreme, or a person, or the Self-Master, or time, or the atom.’

Moreover, Mahamati! There are seven kinds of self-nature: the self-nature of collectedness, the self-nature of own-being, the self-nature of characteristics, the self-nature of the great elements, the self-nature of the cause, the self-nature of the condition, and the self-nature of accomplishment.

Moreover, Mahamati! There are seven kinds of the ultimate truth, namely: the realm of the mind, the realm of insight, the realm of wisdom, the realm of vision, the realm that transcends the two views, the realm that transcends the stage of disciples, and the realm of the Tathagata’s own attainment. Mahamati! This is the mind of ultimate truth and self-nature of the Tathagatas, the worthy ones, the fully enlightened ones of the past, future, and present.
This mind, in Sanskrit, is called ‘hrdaya’; hrdaya in the Chinese translation means the core, like the heart of a tree, not the mind of thought; the mind of thought is in Sanskrit called ‘citta.’

By the mind of ultimate truth and self-nature, the Tathagata accomplishes the worldly, the supramundane, and the supremely supramundane dharmas; the eye of noble wisdom enters the establishing of the self-characteristics and common characteristics; and as they are established, they are not shared with the evil views of the externalist doctrines. Mahamati! How are they shared with the evil views of the externalists? Through the deluded views of one’s own realm, not being aware that what appears is one’s own mind, and the boundaries not being understood. Mahamati! Foolish ordinary beings make the two views their doctrine regarding nature, no-nature, self-nature, and the ultimate truth.

Moreover, Mahamati! The extinguishing of the suffering of the three realms of existence arises from deluded thought; the extinguishing of the conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma; and the seeing of the illusory realms that appear from one’s own mind — this is what I shall now speak of. Mahamati! If there are monks or brahmins who wish to make appear the cause and result of the endowed and the unendowed, and the dwelling of things in time, and the arising and dwelling of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, or who say that what has arisen then ceases — Mahamati! If they hold to continuity, or things, or arising, or existence, or nirvana, or the path, or karma, or fruit, or truths, so as to destroy them, this is the doctrine of annihilation. Why? Because these are not obtainable before one’s eyes, and because the seeing of a beginning is not their portion. Mahamati! It is like a broken bottle, which cannot serve the purpose of a bottle; and like a burnt seed, which cannot serve the purpose of a sprout. So too, Mahamati! If the nature of the aggregates, the elements, and the sense-fields has already ceased, ceases now, or will cease, then because the deluded thoughts of self-mind see no cause, there is no successive arising for them. Mahamati! If one again speaks of a consciousness of both endowed and unendowed nature, arising from the conjunction of three conditions, then a tortoise should grow hair, and sand should yield oil. Your system would then be refuted, contrary to the definitive meaning. The doctrine of endowed and unendowed has such faults, and the acts and affairs it performs are all empty of meaning. Mahamati! Those externalists who speak of arising from the conjunction of three conditions — their expedients, causes and results, self-characteristics, past, future, and present, endowed and unendowed characteristics — since the beginning have been handed down as accomplished matters; turning in the ground of consciousness and thought, and following the habitual tendencies of their own wrong views, they speak thus. So, Mahamati! Foolish ordinary beings, harmed by evil views, confused and intoxicated by what is crooked, without wisdom, falsely call themselves all-knowing and speak thus. Mahamati! If there are other monks or brahmins who see identity apart from self-nature in what is like a cloud, a fire-wheel, a gandharva-city, unborn things, an illusion, a mirage, the moon in the water, and a dream; who see the inner and outer mind-appearances as the beginningless falsehood of deluded thought, not apart from one’s own mind; with the conditions of deluded thought extinguished, they abandon both deluded speech and that which is spoken, the contemplator and the contemplated; and the store consciousness of the body established by experiences and enjoyments; in the realms of consciousness, the grasper and the grasped being non-corresponding; in the realm of non-existence, apart from arising, dwelling, and ceasing, they enter progressively from their own mind into discrimination. Mahamati! Such a bodhisattva will soon attain the equality of birth and death and nirvana, great compassion and skillful means, and the expedient of non-application. Mahamati! All the realms of sentient beings are all like illusion; without toiling at conditions, he is far from the inner and outer realms, and sees nothing outside the mind. Progressively entering the markless stage, progressively entering from stage to stage the realm of samadhi, he understands the three realms as like illusion, and by discriminating and contemplating, he will attain the samadhi of illusion. He crosses over the non-existence shown by one’s own mind, and abides in the perfection of prajna. He abandons the samadhi of the diamond that comes of the expedients of making, and enters the body of the Tathagata. Entering the transformation of thusness, with spiritual powers at will, compassion and skillful means fully adorned, he enters equally all Buddha-lands, and the abodes of the externalists, apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness. This bodhisattva, progressively turning his body, attains the body of the Tathagata. Mahamati! Therefore, those who wish to attain the body entered by the Tathagata should be far from the mind of the aggregates, the elements, and the sense-fields, the expedients made by conditions, and the falsehood of the deluded thoughts of arising, dwelling, and ceasing. With mind-only directly advancing, observing the fabricated faults of beginningless deluded thought and habitual tendencies, by the thought of the non-existence of the three existences, the unborn Buddha-ground, they reach the realm of their own noble attainment, their own mind at ease, and attain the practice of non-application. Like a wishing-jewel that follows all colors, they enter the subtle minds of sentient beings, and appear as a transformation-body measuring according to their minds, from stage to stage progressively, continuously establishing [the teaching]. Therefore, Mahamati! From my own standpoint this is good, and it should be studied.’

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati again addressed the Buddha, saying: ‘What the World-honored One has spoken of — the mind, intellect, and consciousness, the five dharmas, and the characteristics of self-nature — practiced by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, the self-mind views and the non-conjunction of the realms of objects with what is displayed, all spoken as accomplishing the real characteristic, the heart of all Buddha-words — was spoken for the great bodhisattvas dwelling in the sea-girt Mount Malaya in the Lanka country, and concerns the Dharma-body realm of the store consciousness of the ocean of waves, praised by the Tathagata.’

Then the World-honored One told the bodhisattva Mahamati: ‘Because of four causes the eye-consciousness turns. What are the four? The not being aware of the grasps of one’s own mind as they appear; the habitual tendencies of the beginningless false past forms; the attachment to the nature of consciousness; and the desire to see the various forms. Mahamati! These are the four causes at the place where the water flows, where the store consciousness and the transforming consciousness-waves arise. Mahamati! Just as with the eye-consciousness, all the sense-organs, the atoms, and the pores arise together and, following the realms, arise in due order, so it is likewise. It is like a bright mirror that reflects all forms. Mahamati! It is as when a fierce wind blows upon the great sea: the wind of the external realms stirs the ocean of the mind, and the waves of consciousness are never cut off. Because the characteristics made by the action are neither different nor not-different, and the conditions that unite karma and the arising of characteristics, being deeply attached to, one cannot understand the self-nature of forms and the rest; therefore the five consciousness-bodies turn. Mahamati! Those very five consciousness-bodies, together with their discriminations of the characteristics of the various parts, should be understood as the intellect turning from those same bodies. It does not think: ‘I turn as the mutual cause of one another, from what appears in my own mind, through the attaching of deluded thought.’ But they each, with their destructive characteristics together turning, discriminate the realms, and the divisions of the parts, and this is called their turning. It is like a cultivator who enters the samadhi of contemplation: the subtle habitual tendencies turn without his knowing, and he thinks, ‘The consciousnesses have ceased, and then I enter the meditation of right absorption.’ In fact, it is not that the consciousnesses have ceased and then he enters the absorption; because the seeds of the habitual tendencies are not extinguished, they do not cease; and because with the turning of the realms the grasping is incomplete, they are said to cease. Mahamati! Such being the subtle store consciousness, reaching to its ultimate limit, except for the Tathagatas and the bodhisattvas abiding in the stages, no one can measure it or decide it — not the sravakas, the pratyekabuddhas, nor the samadhi-power attained by the externalists, not their wisdom, their skillful discriminations, or their deciding of the meaning of phrases. When the most excellent and boundless roots of goodness are matured, and one is far from the falsehood of the deluded thoughts of one’s own mind, dwelling in forests and mountains, cultivating according to the lower, middle, and higher [practice], one can see the stream of the deluded thoughts of one’s own mind, receive the anointing of the Buddhas of the immeasurable lands, and attain the power of freedom and the samadhi of spiritual powers. The good spiritual friends, the Buddha-sons and their retinues — the mind, intellect, and consciousness, the realm of self-nature shown by one’s own mind, the false thoughts, the sea of birth and death, karma, craving, and ignorance, all such causes — he entirely transcends. Therefore, Mahamati! All cultivators should draw near to the most excellent spiritual friend.’
Then the World-honored One, wishing to proclaim again the meaning of this, spoke a verse:
As with the mighty ocean’s waves, that by a furious wind are roused,
The great billows heave in the dark sea, and never for a moment pause.
The store consciousness-sea abides changeless, while the wind of realms doth stir,
The various waves of consciousness, leaping and turning, rise and occur.
The blue and red and diverse hues, the conch-shell, milk, and honeyed sweet,
The various tastes, the flowers and fruits, the sun and moon and lights that meet,
Neither different nor not different. When the sea-water stirs its waves,
The seven consciousnesses are likewise, born with the mind as concord makes.
As when the sea-water is transformed, and all its waves revolve and turn,
The seven consciousnesses are likewise, with the mind in concord born.
In that abode, the store consciousness, all the consciousnesses turn and flow.
Through that same intellect, which ponders the meanings of all marks below,
Unbroken marks there are but eight; and the markless is also markless too.
As with the ocean and its waves, there is no difference to be found;
So are the consciousnesses and mind; a difference cannot be obtained.
The mind is named the collector-karma; the intellect, the wide collector-gate;
The consciousnesses and what they know, as the present realms, the five they state.
Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, in verse, put his question:
The blue and red and various forms — from beings all consciousnesses rise;
Like waves, the various dharmas rise; how so? we pray you now advise.”
Then the World-honored One answered in verse:
The blue and red and mixed colors — within the waves there is none at all,
‘The collector-karma’ is said of the mind, to awaken the ignorant common folk.
That karma has no existence at all; from the grasped of one’s own mind apart,
The grasped, and that which nothing grasps, with those waves are one and the same.
The body with its enjoyments and establishment, is the manifesting consciousness of beings,
In it all karmas are revealed, like the waves upon the water’s springs.”
Then the bodhisattva Mahamati again spoke a verse:
The nature of the great sea and its waves, heaving, can be distinguished;
The store and karma are even so; why are they not perceived and known?”
Ordinary beings, without wisdom, have the store-consciousness as the great sea,
The karma-marks are like its waves; by this simile the meaning is conveyed.”
The sun arises and its light shines equally on the low, the middle, and the high;
The Tathagata illumines the world, and for the foolish speaks the real,
Having divided all the dharmas, why does he not the real reveal?”
Then the World-honored One answered in verse:
If one speaks of the real, that mind itself has no reality.
Like the ocean’s waves, an image in a mirror, and a dream,
All these appear at once; the realm of the mind is the same.
Because the realms are not complete, karma turns and is born in due order,
Consciousness is what consciousness cognizes; the intellect, what the intellect intends,
The five are manifested, without any fixed sequence.
As a skilled painter, together with his pupils in the art,
Spread colors and depict all forms; so also do I speak my part.
The colors have no patterns in themselves; not the brush, nor the canvas white,
But to delight the living beings, they interweave and paint the many forms.
Words and speech are separately applied; the real is free of name,
Discrimination answers to the first acts; practice reveals the real.
The real is the place of self-awakening, where thought and its object are apart;
This for the Buddha’s sons is spoken; the foolish spread wide their discriminations.
All the various are like illusion; though they appear, no real is there,
And thus the many teachings, according to matters, are set forth here and there,
What is spoken is not that which is fit; and for such a one it is not speech.
To each and every patient, the good physician orders his prescription,
And the Tathagata, for the sake of beings, according to their minds speaks in due measure.
Deluded thought is not the realm, nor the portion even of the sravakas,
It is what the compassionate one speaks: the realm of self-awakening.

Moreover, Mahamati! If a great bodhisattva wishes to know the measure of the self-mind as it appears, and the realm of the deluded thoughts of the grasper and the grasped, he should be far from the crowd and the common customs, and from sleep; in the first, middle, and last parts of the night he should constantly be self-awakening and cultivate the expedient means; he should be far from the books and the words of the evil doctrines, and from the characteristics of the sravaka and the pratyekabuddha vehicles; and he should thoroughly understand the marks of the deluded thoughts that appear from his own mind.

Moreover, Mahamati! When a great bodhisattva has established the characteristic of abiding in wisdom, he should diligently study the three characteristics of the supreme noble wisdom. What are the three characteristics of the supreme noble wisdom that should be diligently studied? The characteristic of the realm of non-existence, the characteristic of the place of the self-vows of all Buddhas, and the characteristic of the ultimate attainment of self-realized noble wisdom. Having cultivated and obtained these, he can abandon the heart of the lame donkey with its characteristics of wisdom and insight, attain the eighth stage of the most excellent sons, and then cultivate and produce the practice of those three characteristics above. Mahamati! The characteristic of the realm of non-existence means the characteristics of the sravakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the externalists, which are produced by their own cultivation. Mahamati! The characteristic of the place of the self-vows means what is produced by cultivating in the place of the self-vows of the Buddhas of the past. Mahamati! The characteristic of the ultimate attainment of self-realized noble wisdom means, without attachment to any characteristic of dharmas, obtaining the body of the samadhi of illusion and advancing into the stage of the Buddha-ground through practice. Mahamati! These are called the three characteristics of noble wisdom. If one accomplishes these three characteristics of noble wisdom, he can reach the realm of self-realized noble wisdom. Therefore, Mahamati! The three characteristics of noble wisdom should be diligently studied.”

Then the great bodhisattva Mahamati, knowing what the assembly of great bodhisattvas had in mind, and calling it the scripture that distinguishes the self-nature of the matter of noble wisdom, relying upon the awe-inspiring power of all the Buddhas, addressed the Buddha, saying: ‘World-honored One, we pray you to expound the scripture that distinguishes the self-nature of the matter of noble wisdom, the basis of the discriminations of the one hundred and eight phrases. The Tathagata, the worthy one, the fully enlightened one, according to this, by discrimination, teaches the great bodhisattvas to enter the self-characteristics, the common characteristics, and the self-nature of deluded thought. By expounding the self-nature of deluded thought through discrimination, they can know well, everywhere observing, the egolessness of persons and of dharmas, purify deluded thought, illumine all the stages, transcend all the joys of the meditative concentrations of the sravakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the externalists, observe the inconceivable realm of the Tathagata’s practice, and ultimately abandon the five dharmas and self-nature. The wisdom of the Dharma-body of the Buddhas and Tathagatas, well self-adorned, transcending the realm of illusion, rising to all Buddha-lands, the Tushita palace, even to the Akanistha palace, they attain the eternally abiding Dharma-body of the Tathagata.’

The Buddha told Mahamati: ‘There is a class of externalists who, taking hold of the deluded thought of non-existence, and seeing the causes exhausted, conceive that the hare has no horns. As the hare has no horns, so too are all dharmas. Mahamati! There are yet other externalists who, seeing the seeds, the qualities, the atoms, and the forms of the elements and their various differences, and having seen them, take hold of the erroneous dharma that the hare has no horns, and conceive that the cow has horns. Mahamati! They fall into the two views, not understanding the measure of the mind; within the realm of their own mind the deluded thoughts of the body and its enjoyments grow, and they establish the limits of deluded thought. Mahamati! The nature of all dharmas is likewise: apart from existence and non-existence, one should not entertain such a thought. Mahamati! If, apart from existence and non-existence, one makes the thought that the hare has no horns, this is called an erroneous thought. Because of the dependent observation, the hare has no horns; but one should not entertain that thought, even to the atoms, wherein the nature of things is discriminated and all is unobtainable. Mahamati! The holy realm is apart from this; one should not conceive that the cow has horns.’ Then the great bodhisattva Mahamati addressed the Buddha, saying: ‘World-honored One, does one who is free of deluded thought, having seen the non-arising of thought and following it in reasoning and observing that non-arising of deluded thought, speak of non-existence?’

The Buddha told Mahamati: ‘It is not by observing the non-arising of thought that one speaks of non-existence. Why? Because deluded thought arises because of that; it arises depending on horns. Because deluded thought arises depending on horns, therefore it is spoken of as relying on a cause; and so, apart from different and not-different, it is not by observing the non-arising of thought that one speaks of the hare’s having no horns. Mahamati! If deluded thought were different from horns, it would not arise because of horns; if it were not different, then it would arise because of them. Even analyzing the atoms and seeking throughout, all is unobtainable, being not different from horns. That also is not a nature; if both have no nature, then what dharma, and for what reason, does one speak of non-existence? Mahamati! If because of non-existence there are no horns, and observing existence one says the hare has no horns, one should not entertain that thought. Mahamati! Since it is not a right cause, speaking of existence and non-existence, both are not established. Mahamati! There are yet other externalists who, viewing the empty nature of form as a matter of shape and place, and the erroneous dharmas, cannot know well the divisions of space, saying form is apart from space, and giving rise to the deluded thoughts of division. Mahamati! Space is form, entering the class of form. Mahamati! Form is that which space holds, established in the place held; the nature of form and the empty matter, by discrimination, should be known. Mahamati! When the four great elements arise, their self-characteristics are each distinct, and they do not dwell in space, yet it is not that there is no space. So, Mahamati! Observing that the cow has horns, therefore the hare has none. Mahamati! Again, the cow’s horns, broken into atoms, and again the atoms discriminated, not abiding for an instant — what is it that is observed because of which one speaks of non-existence? If one says it observes some other thing, that dharma is likewise.’

Then the World-honored One told the great bodhisattva Mahamati: ‘You should be far from the hare’s horns and the cow’s horns, from space and form and color, and the deluded thoughts of different views. You great bodhisattvas should contemplate the deluded thoughts that appear from your own minds, and entering [all lands] as the most excellent sons of all the realms, teach them by the expedient of what appears from your own mind.’
Form and the rest, and the mind, are without; yet form and the rest nurture the mind,
The body, its enjoyments and establishment, in the store consciousness exhibit beings.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness; the self-nature dharmas are five,
The two kinds of purity of no-self, spoken by the expounder vast.
Long, short, existence, non-existence, and the rest, mutually arise and turn around,
By non-existence existence becomes; by existence, non-existence is found.
The atoms and the discriminating affairs — no deluded thought of form arises there,
The place where the measure of the mind is established — the erroneous views do not delight.
Thought and perception is not the realm; the sravakas likewise are the same,
It is what the saviour of the world speaks: the realm of self-awakening attained.”

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, for the sake of purifying the streams that appear from his own mind, again requested the Tathagata, saying: ‘World-honored One, how does one purify the streams that appear from the minds of all sentient beings? Is it instantaneous or gradual?’

The Buddha told Mahamati: ‘It is a gradual purification, not instantaneous. As with the amra fruit, which ripens gradually and not at once; the Tathagata’s purification of the streams appearing from the minds of all sentient beings is likewise: a gradual purification, not instantaneous. As a potter makes the various vessels, completing them gradually and not at once; the Tathagata’s purification of the streams appearing from the minds of all sentient beings is likewise: a gradual purification, not instantaneous. As the great earth gradually produces the myriad things, and not all at once; the Tathagata’s purification of the streams appearing from the minds of all sentient beings is likewise: a gradual purification, not instantaneous. As a person learns music, painting, writing, and the various arts, completing them gradually and not at once; the Tathagata’s purification of the streams that appear from the minds of all sentient beings is likewise: a gradual purification, not instantaneous. As a bright mirror instantly reveals all the markless forms and images; the Tathagata’s purification of the streams that appear from the minds of all sentient beings is likewise: instantly revealing the markless, the non-existent, the pure realm. As the wheel of the sun and the wheel of the moon instantly shine forth and reveal all forms and images; the Tathagata, for the beings who are free of the faults of the habitual tendencies appearing from their own minds, is likewise: instantly revealing the most excellent realm of the inconceivable wisdom. As the store consciousness instantly discriminates and knows what appears from one’s own mind and the realm of the body’s establishment and enjoyments; those dependent Buddhas are likewise,
‘Dependent’ in the Sanskrit text is ‘nirmita’; the meaning is that the transformation-Buddha is the very breath and essential portion of the real Buddha.

instantly ripening the realms where beings abide, so that cultivators are placed in that Akanistha heaven. As the dependent Buddha made by the Dharma-Buddha, radiating light and shining; the realm of self-realized noble attainment is likewise, and as for the deluded thoughts of the evil views regarding the marks of dharmas, of having a nature and no-nature, it shines upon them and causes them to be eradicated. Mahamati! The Dharma-dependent Buddha speaks all dharmas, entering the cause of the self-characteristics and common characteristics, of the habitual tendencies appearing from one’s own mind, the cause of the continuous deluded thoughts of the attachment to the self-nature, the various unreal illusions, the various attachments, all unobtainable.

Moreover, Mahamati! The attachment to the self-nature of dependent arising gives rise to the characteristics of the self-nature of deluded thought. Mahamati! As a skilled illusionist, depending on grass, trees, tiles, and stones, produces various illusions, and causes beings to arise in various forms and colors, giving rise to all manner of deluded thoughts; those deluded thoughts too have no reality. So, Mahamati! Depending on the self-nature of dependent arising, there arises the self-nature of deluded thought. The various deluded thoughts, the various particular thoughts and the characteristics of their activity, the deluded thoughts of the attachment to the habitual tendencies — Mahamati! This is the arising of the characteristics of the self-nature of deluded thought. Mahamati! This is called the Dharma preaching of the dependent Buddha. Mahamati! The Dharma-Buddha is apart from the self-nature and the characteristics of the mind, and in the realm of the object of self-realized noble wisdom, establishes and accomplishes. Mahamati! The transformation-Buddha speaks of giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and the wisdom of the mind. Apart from the aggregates, the sense-fields, and the elements, freed from the discriminations of the characteristics of consciousness; observing and establishing, transcending the views of the externalists, transcending the view of form. Mahamati! Again, the Dharma-Buddha is apart from attachment, free of the object, all the marks of the measures of the activity of the sense-organs ceasing; not the realm to which the ordinary beings, the sravakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the externalists, attached to the marks of self, cling; the realm of self-realized noble wisdom’s ultimate and distinctive marks is established. Therefore, Mahamati! The distinctive marks of self-realized noble wisdom should be diligently studied, and the appearances of one’s own mind should be eradicated.

Moreover, Mahamati! There are two kinds of sravaka vehicles distinguished by their characteristic marks: the characteristic of attaining the self-realized noble distinctiveness, and the characteristic of attachment to the self-nature of the nature of deluded thought. How is the sravaka said to have attained the characteristic of self-realized noble distinctiveness? It is the realm of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and no-self. The ultimate truth, free of desire, still; the self and common characteristics of the aggregates, the elements, and the sense-fields quiesced; the external unbroken marks known as they are; the mind attains stillness. The mind being still, the meditative concentration, the liberation, the samadhi, the fruit of the path, the right absorption and liberation; yet not free of the habitual tendencies, and of the inconceivable transformation-death, obtains the sravaka who abides in the joy of self-realized noble wisdom; this is called the sravaka who has attained the characteristic of self-realized noble distinctiveness. Mahamati! A great bodhisattva who attains the abode of the joy of self-realized noble distinctiveness does not delight in the joy of the state of extinction, the joy of right absorption, but out of pity for sentient beings and by his original vow, does not realize [that state]. Mahamati! This is called the joy of the sravaka who has attained the characteristic of self-realized noble distinctiveness. A great bodhisattva should not study the joy of that sravaka who has attained the characteristic of self-realized noble distinctiveness. Mahamati! How is the sravaka said to have the characteristic of attachment to the self-nature of the nature of deluded thought? It is the great elements: blue, yellow, red, white; hard, wet, warm, moving; not made, yet arising with self-characteristics and common characteristics. Having seen these, as first set forth by the former worthy ones, he gives rise to the deluded thought of self-nature regarding them. A great bodhisattva should know them and abandon them, entering the thought of the egolessness of dharmas, extinguishing the view of the ego of persons, and progressively from stage to stage continuously establishing [the teaching]; this is called the characteristic of the sravakas’ attachment to the self-nature of the nature of deluded thought.”

Then the great bodhisattva Mahamati addressed the Buddha, saying: ‘World-honored One, with respect to what the World-honored One has spoken of — the eternal and the inconceivable, the realm of self-realized noble attainment and the realm of the ultimate truth — World-honored One, is it not the eternal and inconceivable cause spoken of by the externalists?’

The Buddha told Mahamati: ‘It is not by the causes of the externalists that the eternal and inconceivable is obtained. Why? Because the eternal and inconceivable of the externalists is not accomplished by means of their own characteristic. If the eternal and inconceivable is not accomplished by means of their own characteristic, then by what cause is the eternal and inconceivable manifested?

Moreover, Mahamati! If the inconceivable were accomplished by means of its own characteristic, then it would be eternal. But because of the characteristic of a maker as a cause, the eternal and inconceivable is not accomplished. Mahamati! My ultimate truth is the eternal and inconceivable. It is accomplished by the cause of the ultimate truth’s characteristic, apart from nature and no-nature, and because it attains the self-realized characteristic, it has a mark. Because it is the cause of the wisdom of the ultimate truth, it has a cause apart from nature and no-nature. It is like unconditioned space, eternal because of the extinction of nirvana. So, Mahamati! It is different from the doctrine of the eternal and inconceivable of the externalists. So, Mahamati! This eternal and inconceivable is what the Tathagatas have obtained by self-realized noble wisdom; therefore, this eternal and inconceivable, obtained by self-realized noble wisdom, should be studied.

Moreover, Mahamati! The eternal and inconceivable of the externalists has the nature of impermanence. Because it is the cause of a different characteristic, and not from the power of the characteristic of its own cause, it is not eternal.

Moreover, Mahamati! The eternal and inconceivable of the externalists: with regard to the nature of what is made, being and no-being being impermanent, having seen this, they reason and conceive it as eternal. Mahamati! I likewise, with this cause and condition, [see] what is made as having the nature of being and no-being, as impermanent; and seeing this, within the realm of self-realized noble wisdom, I speak of their eternal as having no cause. Mahamati! If again the externalists, by the cause of their characteristics, accomplish the eternal and inconceivable, then by the self-nature of their own characteristic, being and no-being, it is the same as the hare’s horns. This eternal and inconceivable is but a deluded thought of words. The externalists have such a fault. Why? Because it is merely verbal deluded thought, like the hare’s horns, and their own cause and characteristic is not their portion. Mahamati! My eternal and inconceivable, being obtained by the self-realized characteristic, and apart from the nature of what is made and its being and no-being, is eternal. It is not the impermanence of external nature and no-nature, reasoned and conceived as eternal. Mahamati! If again, regarding external nature and no-nature as impermanent, one reasons and conceives the eternal and inconceivable as eternal, and that person does not know the self-cause and characteristic of the eternal and inconceivable, he is far from the characteristic of the realm of self-realized noble wisdom. He should not so speak.

Moreover, Mahamati! The sravakas, fearing the suffering of the deluded thoughts of birth and death, seek nirvana, but they do not know that the discrimination between birth and death and nirvana, in the nature of all things, is a deluded thought with no real nature. The peaceful ending of the future sense-organs and their realms, they make into the thought of nirvana, not realizing that it is the turning of the store consciousness toward the realm of self-realized noble wisdom. Therefore, ordinary fools say there are three vehicles, and speak of the measure of the mind attaining non-existence. Therefore, Mahamati! They do not know that what appears from the minds of the Tathagatas of the past, future, and present is a realm of their own mind, and they cling to the realm appearing from an external mind, and the wheel of birth and death turns forever.

Moreover, Mahamati! All dharmas are unborn; this is what the Tathagatas of the past, future, and present have spoken. Why? Because the self-nature of what appears in one’s own mind has no nature, being apart from the arising of existence and non-existence. Mahamati! All natures are unborn; all dharmas are like the horns of a hare or a horse, which are the false deluded thoughts of foolish ordinary beings, of their unreal self-nature. Mahamati! All dharmas are unborn; in the realm of the path of self-realized noble wisdom, the self-nature and the mark of all natures are unborn — not the two realms of the deluded thoughts of those foolish ones. The self-nature, the body, and the possessions are established from the self-nature of the path. Mahamati! When the store consciousness, and what it holds and what is held, turn, the foolish fall into the two views of birth, abiding, and ceasing, and long for the arising of all natures. The deluded thoughts of existence and non-existence arise, and they are not noble ones. Mahamati! This should be studied.

Moreover, Mahamati! There are five non-interrupted spiritual lineages. What are the five? The non-interrupted lineage of the sravaka vehicle, the non-interrupted lineage of the pratyekabuddha vehicle, the non-interrupted lineage of the Tathagata vehicle, the indeterminate lineage, and the distinct lineage. How is the non-interrupted lineage of the sravaka vehicle known? If, upon hearing the teaching of cutting off the self and common characteristics of the aggregates, the sense-fields, and the elements, one’s whole body and pores are thrilled with joy and gladness, and one delights in the wisdom of the characteristics of cultivation but does not cultivate the awakening of dependent origination, this is called the non-interrupted lineage of the sravaka vehicle. The sravaka’s non-interrupted [practice] sees the eighth stage, and the afflictions arising are cut off, but the habitual afflictions are not cut off. He does not transcend the inconceivable transformation-death, but transcends the divided death. He roars the lion’s roar: ‘My birth has ended, the pure life has been established, and there is no further existence.’ Knowing truly, he cultivates the egolessness of persons, and even attains the realization of nirvana. Mahamati! As for the distinct non-interrupted lineage: self, person, beings, life, the nourishing, the person — those beings make this realization and seek nirvana. There are also other externalists who say everything comes from a maker. Having seen all natures, they say: ‘This is nirvana.’ Making this realization, not seeing the egolessness of dharmas, they have no liberation. Mahamati! These non-interrupted lineages of the sravaka vehicle and the externalists do not go out of the re-arising of existence. To turn them away from those evil views, one should study. Mahamati! As for the non-interrupted lineage of the pratyekabuddha vehicle: if, upon hearing the teaching of the separate conditions of the non-interrupted [lineage], one’s hair stands on end and one weeps, and one is not near to the conditions, and is not attached to anything, and delights in the various bodies, the various spiritual powers, separation and union, and the various transformations — hearing this, his mind enters it. If one knows the non-interrupted lineage of the pratyekabuddha vehicle, one accords with it and speaks of the pratyekabuddha vehicle; this is called the characteristic of the non-interrupted lineage of the pratyekabuddha vehicle. Mahamati! As for the non-interrupted lineage of the Tathagata vehicle, there are four [kinds]: the non-interrupted lineage of the self-nature of dharmas, the non-interrupted lineage of the dharmas apart from self-characteristics, the non-interrupted lineage of the attainment of self-realized noble wisdom, and the non-interrupted lineage of the excellence of the other realms. Mahamati! If, upon hearing each of these four things spoken, and upon hearing of the inconceivable realm of the body, the possessions, and the establishment appearing from one’s own mind, his mind does not tremble with fear — this is called the characteristic of the non-interrupted lineage of the Tathagata vehicle. Mahamati! As for the indeterminate lineage: when those three are spoken of, according to what is spoken he enters it, and according to that he becomes. Mahamati! This is [taught] for those first in the stage of cultivation; that is, the establishment of the lineages, in order to transcend and enter the stage of non-existence, is so established. The one who realizes the store himself, his own afflictions and habitual tendencies being pure, sees the egolessness of dharmas, obtains the joy of samadhi as a sravaka, and will attain the most excellent body of the Tathagata.”
Then the World-honored One, wishing to proclaim again the meaning of this, spoke a verse:
The fruit of Srotapanna, of the once-returner, and of the non-returner,
And attaining Arhatship — these are in a mind confused.
The three vehicles and the one vehicle, and the no-vehicle I have spoken,
The foolish, with little wisdom; the sages afar and still.
The Dharma-gate of the ultimate truth is far from the two teachings,
Abiding in non-existence, how should the three vehicles be established?
All the meditations, measureless, the formless samadhi,
Feeling and perception wholly quenched, and there is no measure of the mind.

Mahamati! Those icchantikas are not [truly] icchantikas. Who turns [the wheel of] the world and liberation? Mahamati! There are two kinds of icchantikas: one who abandons all roots of goodness, and one who, from the beginningless [past], makes vows for sentient beings. What is abandoning all roots of goodness? To slander the bodhisattva-treasury, and to make evil statements such as: ‘This is not in accord with the teaching of the sutras, the vinaya, and liberation.’ Because he abandons all roots of goodness, he does not attain nirvana. Second, because of the bodhisattva’s own original vow of skillful means, it is not that all sentient beings do not attain nirvana, but that he attains nirvana [for them]. Mahamati! That nirvana is called the characteristic of the dharma of not-nirvana. This too reaches the state of the icchantika.”
Mahamati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One! In this [teaching], how is it that one ultimately does not enter parinirvana?"

The Buddha told Mahamati: "The bodhisattva-icchantika, having known that all dharmas are originally in parinirvana, ultimately does not enter parinirvana; he is not an icchantika who has abandoned all roots of good. Mahamati! The icchantika who has abandoned all roots of good, by reason of the Tathagata's spiritual power, may at times have his roots of good arise. Why is this? Because the Tathagata does not abandon any living being. For this reason the bodhisattva-icchantika does not enter parinirvana.

Moreover, Mahamati! The bodhisattva-mahasattva should be skillful with regard to the three self-natures. What are the three self-natures? They are the imagined self-nature, the dependent self-nature, and the accomplished self-nature. Mahamati! The imagined self-nature arises from marks."
Mahamati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One! How does the imagined self-nature arise from marks?"

The Buddha told Mahamati: "The dependent self-nature as to marks of things, and the marks of things as manifested in processes, gives rise to two kinds of imagined self-nature through attachment. What is established by the Tathagata, Arhat, Fully-Enlightened One, is the mark of attachment to name and mark, and the mark of attachment to thing and mark. The mark of attachment to name and mark is attachment to inner and outer dharmas. The mark of attachment to thing and mark is attachment to the self-marks and common-marks of those very inner and outer dharmas. These are called the marks of the two kinds of imagined self-nature. What arises depending upon a basis and upon conditions is called dependent [self-nature]. What is the accomplished self-nature? It is that which is apart from the imagining of name-mark and thing-mark, attained by noble wisdom, and the realm of practice entered by self-realized noble wisdom; this is called the accomplished self-nature, the Tathagata-garbha mind."
Then the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Name and mark, perceiving and imagining, the two marks of self-nature, right knowledge and thusness,
these are then the accomplished mark.

Mahamati! This is called the sutra on contemplating the marks of the self-natures of the five dharmas, the realm of practice entered by self-realized noble wisdom. You bodhisattvas-mahasattvas should study it."

Moreover, Mahamati! The bodhisattva-mahasattva rightly contemplates the marks of the two kinds of selflessness. What are the two kinds of selflessness? They are the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of dharmas. What is the selflessness of persons? It is being free of self and what belongs to self, and free of the aggregates, elements, and entrances. From ignorance, action, and craving are born; grasping at forms, sounds, and the rest gives rise to consciousness; all the faculties, the body as the vessel of what is self-manifested in the mind, are set forth and displayed by the mind's own imagined marks. Like a river, like a seed, like a lamp, like wind, like a cloud, they are destroyed in an instant, turning one upon another. Restless as a monkey, delighting in impure places as a fly, insatiable as wind and fire, [bound] by the causes of beginningless false habitual tendencies as by a water-drawing wheel. Turning through the wheel of the realms of birth-and-death, taking on all manner of bodies and forms, like conjurations and mantras, like a mechanism set in motion and an image that arises. Knowing well those marks is called the wisdom of the selflessness of persons. What is the wisdom of the selflessness of dharmas? It is realizing that the aggregates, elements, and entrances are the imagined marks of a self-nature that is thusness, that the aggregates, elements, and entrances are free of self and of what belongs to self. The aggregates, elements, and entrances, being heaped together, bound by the rope of action and craving, turning upon one another by conditions, arise without moving. Likewise all dharmas, being free of self-marks and common-marks. The unreal imagined marks and the power of imagining are what arise for the ordinary man, not for the sages, because of being free of mind, consciousness, the five dharmas, and the self-natures. Mahamati! The bodhisattva-mahasattva should rightly discriminate that all dharmas are selfless. Being skillful in the selflessness of dharmas, the bodhisattva-mahasattva before long attains the bodhisattva's first-stage contemplation of the nonexistence of anything. Observing the ground-marks, he awakens and rejoices. Advancing step by step, he passes beyond the marks of the nine stages and attains the Dharma-cloud stage. There he establishes the immeasurably jewel-adorned great lotus-king image, the great jewel-palace, which arises through the cultivation of the realm of the imaginary self-nature's transformations, and there he sits. Surrounded by the noble offspring of the same class, who come from all Buddha-lands, the Buddha's hand anoints [his head], as the crown prince of a wheel-turning sage-king is anointed. Passing beyond the stage of Buddha-sons, he reaches the Dharma-trend of self-realization and attains the Tathagata's sovereign Dharma-body. Because he sees the selflessness of dharmas, this is called the mark of the selflessness of dharmas. You bodhisattvas-mahasattvas should study it."

Then the bodhisattva-mahasattva Mahamati again said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One! The marks of establishment and of slander, may you be pleased to speak of them, so that I and all the bodhisattvas-mahasattvas may be free of the two extremes of evil views, establishment and slander, and quickly attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Having awakened, being free of the views of eternalist establishment and nihilist slander, we will no longer slander the right Dharma." Then the World-Honored One, having accepted the request of Mahamati the bodhisattva, spoke these verses:
Establishment and slander, there is no mind-measure there,
the establishment of body, pleasure, and possession, and the mind cannot know it,
the foolish without wisdom, [fall into] establishment and slander."

Then the World-Honored One, again further displaying the meaning of this verse, told Mahamati: "There are four kinds of establishment of what is nonexistent as existent. What are the four? They are: the establishment of a nonexistent mark, the establishment of a nonexistent view, the establishment of a nonexistent cause, and the establishment of a nonexistent nature. These are called the four kinds of establishment. Moreover, as to slander: with regard to what is established, having no attainment, observing it as not being the case, one gives rise to slander. These are called the marks of establishment and slander.

Moreover, Mahamati! What is the mark of the establishment of a nonexistent mark? It is that the aggregates, elements, and entrances, having no self-marks or common-marks, yet one gives rise to attachment, saying "this is thus, this is not different." This is called the mark of the establishment of a nonexistent mark. This imagining of the establishment of a nonexistent mark arises from the fault of beginningless falsehood and the attachment to various habitual tendencies. Mahamati! As to the mark of the establishment of a nonexistent view: if one establishes, with regard to those very aggregates, elements, and entrances, the views of self, person, being, life-span, sustaining one, and the man, this is called the mark of the establishment of a nonexistent view. Mahamati! As to the mark of the establishment of a nonexistent cause: it is that the first consciousness arises without a cause, and afterward what is unreal, like an illusion, is originally unarisen. Thought [in], eye, form, and eye-realm arise; having arisen and become real, they again undergo destruction. This is called the mark of the establishment of a nonexistent cause. Mahamati! As to the mark of the establishment of a nonexistent nature: it is establishing a nature through attachment to space, extinction, parinirvana, and the non-made. This is free of nature and of non-nature; all dharmas are like the horns of a hare or a horse, like hair seen in a vision, free of existence and nonexistence; this is called the mark of the establishment of a nonexistent nature. Establishment and slander are the imagining of the foolish, who do not rightly contemplate the presented measure of their own mind; they are not sages. Therefore, being free of the evil views of establishment and slander, one should study it."

Moreover, Mahamati! The bodhisattva-mahasattva, being skillful in the mind, the will, and consciousness, the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the marks of the two selflessnesses, reaches the ultimate. For the peace and benefit of beings, he displays all kinds of forms, as in the imaginary self-nature he relies upon the dependent [self-nature]. For example, the wish-fulfilling jewel of many colors universally appears in all the Buddha-fields, and in all the great assemblies of the Tathagatas, [beings] hear the sutras and Dharma within it. So-called: all dharmas are like an illusion, like a dream, like shadow and reflection, like the moon in water; in all dharmas he is free of arising and ceasing, of eternality and annihilation, and free of the dharmas of the voice-hearers and pratyekabuddhas, attaining hundreds and thousands of samadhis, even hundreds of thousands of kośi of nayutas of samadhis. Having attained the samadhis, he roams the Buddha-fields and makes offerings to the Buddhas. He is born in the palaces of the heavens and proclaims the Three Jewels. He manifests a Buddha-body, surrounded by the great assemblies of voice-hearers and bodhisattvas, and with the presented measure of his own mind delivers and frees beings, discriminating and expounding that the nature of external things is without self-nature, causing them all to be free of the views of existence and nonexistence."
Then the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The mind-measure is the world, the Buddha-son observes; the body of the various kinds,
free of the deeds that are done, he gains transcendent power and accomplishes sovereignty."

Then the bodhisattva-mahasattva Mahamati again requested the Buddha: "May the World-Honored One be pleased to teach us the emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and freedom from self-nature of all dharmas. When we and the other bodhisattvas have awakened to this emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and freedom from self-nature, being free of the imagining of existence and nonexistence, we will quickly attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."
Then the World-Honored One told Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva: "Listen! Listen! Think of it well in mind. Now I will for you set it forth in detail."
Mahamati said to the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One! I will gladly receive the teaching."

The Buddha told Mahamati: "The emptiness of emptiness is precisely the place of the imagined self-nature. Mahamati! Those attached to the imagined self-nature are told of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and freedom from self-nature. Mahamati! Briefly, there are seven kinds of emptiness. They are: the emptiness of marks, the emptiness of self-nature, the emptiness of processes, the emptiness of non-processes, the emptiness of all dharmas as free of speech, the great emptiness of the noble wisdom of ultimate truth, and the emptiness of that-in-which-there-is-no-that. What is the emptiness of marks? It is that the self-marks and common-marks of all natures are empty, because of contemplating their mutual heaping-together; discriminating their selfless nature, the self-marks and common-marks do not arise. Both self and other are of a nature that is without nature, therefore the marks do not abide; and so it is said that the marks of all natures are empty. This is called the emptiness of marks. What is the emptiness of self-nature? It is that a thing's own self-nature does not arise of itself; this is called the emptiness of the self-nature of all dharmas. Therefore it is said to be the emptiness of self-nature. What is the emptiness of processes? It is that the aggregates, being free of self and what belongs to self, that which is accomplished by causes, and that which is produced through the activity of actions and conventions, — this is called the emptiness of processes. Mahamati! This very emptiness of processes, in which the dependent, conditioned self-nature is without self-nature, is called the emptiness of non-processes. What is the emptiness of all dharmas as free of speech? It is that the imagined self-nature has no speech, and therefore all dharmas are free of speech; this is called the emptiness of all dharmas as free of speech. What is the great emptiness of the noble wisdom of the ultimate truth of all dharmas? It is that, having attained self-realized noble wisdom, the habitual tendencies of the fault of all views are empty; this is called the great emptiness of the noble wisdom of the ultimate truth of all dharmas. What is the emptiness of that-in-which-there-is-no-that? It is that in that [place] it is empty of that [thing]; this is called the emptiness of that-in-which-there-is-no-that. Mahamati! For example, the deer-mother's house: it is empty of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep, [but] not free of [the presence of] monks; and yet one speaks of that emptiness. It is not that the house-nature is empty, nor is the bhikshu-nature empty; nor is it that elsewhere there are no elephants and horses; this is called the self-marks of all dharmas. That in that [place] there is not that [thing] is called the emptiness of that-in-which-there-is-no-that. These are called the seven kinds of emptiness. The emptiness of that-in-which-there-is-no-that is the coarsest of emptinesses; you should stay far from it. Mahamati! Not self-arising, yet not non-arising; apart from dwelling in samadhi, this is called non-arising. Being free of self-nature is itself non-arising. Being free of self-nature, and the instant-by-instant continuous flow and the appearance of different natures — all natures being free of self-nature, therefore all natures are free of self-nature. What is non-duality? It is that all dharmas, like cold and heat, like long and short, like black and white. Mahamati! All dharmas are non-dual: it is not that in nirvana there is that birth-and-death, nor that in birth-and-death there is that nirvana. Because the marks of difference are of one nature, this is called non-duality. Like nirvana and birth-and-death, so too are all dharmas. Therefore the emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and freedom from self-nature should be studied."
Then the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
I always speak the Dharma of emptiness, free from annihilation and eternality,
birth-and-death is like a dream and an illusion, yet that karma is not destroyed.
Space and nirvana, the extinguishing of duality is likewise,
the foolish give rise to imagining; the sages are free of existence and nonexistence."

Then the World-Honored One again told Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva: "Mahamati! Emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and freedom from self-nature universally enter into all the sutras of the Buddhas. Every sutra whatsoever speaks of this meaning. The sutras, following the hopes of beings, set it forth in discriminating fashion, displaying their meaning, yet the true reality does not lie in speech. Like a deer's thirst-thought, which deludes the herd of deer; the deer attach to the water-nature of that mark, yet that water does not exist. Thus all the dharmas spoken of in the sutras, in order to make the foolish rejoice, are not the real noble wisdom that lies in speech. Therefore, one should rely upon the meaning and not cling to speech."

Then the bodhisattva-mahasattva Mahamati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One! The World-Honored One's sutra says that the Tathagata-garbha, self-nature pure, turning the thirty-two marks, enters into the body of all living beings; like a great-price jewel wrapped in a soiled garment. The Tathagata's treasury, ever abiding and unchanging, is also like this, yet it is wrapped in the soiled garment of the aggregates, elements, and entrances, defiled by greed, hatred, and delusion, and the dust and toil of unreal imagining — as taught and set forth by all the Buddhas. How does the World-Honored One, same as the sectarians, speak of a self and say there is a Tathagata-garbha? World-Honored One! The sectarians also speak of an eternal maker, free of the gunas, omnipresent and imperishable. World-Honored One! They speak of a self."

The Buddha told Mahamati: "I speak of the Tathagata-garbha, but it is not the same as the self spoken of by the sectarians. Mahamati! At times I speak of emptiness, marklessness, wishlessness, thusness, reality, Dharmata, the Dharma-body, nirvana, freedom from self-nature, non-arising and non-ceasing, originally still, self-nature nirvana — and with these various phrases I speak of the Tathagata-garbha. The Tathagata, Arhat, Fully-Enlightened One, in order to cut off the foolish people's fear of the phrase "selflessness," speaks of the Tathagata-garbha gate that is free of imagining and of the realm of nothing-at-all. Mahamati! Bodhisattvas-mahasattvas of the future and the present should not make the view of self and cling to it. For example, a potter, from one lump of clay, with the skillful means of human effort, water, wood, a wheel, and a rope, makes all kinds of vessels. The Tathagata is likewise: in the selflessness of dharmas, free of all imagining marks, he uses all kinds of wisdom and skillful means, at times speaking of the Tathagata-garbha, at times speaking of selflessness. For this reason it is said that the Tathagata-garbha is not the same as the self spoken of by the sectarians. This is called speaking of the Tathagata-garbha. To draw in and lead on the sectarians who cling to a self, he speaks of the Tathagata-garbha, causing them to be free of the unreal imagining of the self-view, to enter the realm of the three gates of liberation, and to hope for the quick attainment of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Therefore the Tathagata, Arhat, Fully-Enlightened One speaks thus of the Tathagata-treasury. If it were not so, he would be the same as the self spoken of by the sectarians. Therefore, Mahamati! To be free of the sectarian views, one should rely upon the selfless Tathagata-garbha."
The aggregates of the continuity of person, with conditions and atoms, the sovereign maker,
are mind-measure and imagining."

Then Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva, observing the beings of the future, again requested the World-Honored One: "May [the Buddha] be pleased to speak of the unbroken practice of cultivation, the great skillful means of those bodhisattvas-mahasattvas who cultivate."

The Buddha told Mahamati: "The bodhisattva-mahasattva accomplishing four dharmas attains the great skillful means of the cultivator. What are the four? They are: being skillful in discriminating the present[ation] of his own mind, contemplating the nature of external things as without self-nature, being free of the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing, and attaining the joy of self-realized noble wisdom. These are called the bodhisattva-mahasattva's accomplishment of the four dharmas through which he attains the great skillful means of the cultivator. How does the bodhisattva-mahasattva rightly discriminate the present[ation] of his own mind? It is that he contemplates thus that the three realms are only mind, without boundary, free of self and of what belongs to self, without movement, free of going and coming, yet fumigated by the false habitual tendencies of beginninglessness; the various forms and processes of the three realms, the body, wealth, and what is established, are bound [thereby], and imagining follows in and presents itself. This is called the bodhisattva-mahasattva's right discrimination of the present[ation] of his own mind. How does the bodhisattva-mahasattva rightly contemplate the nature of external things as without self-nature? It is that, as to such natures as a mirage and a dream, [he sees] the causes of beginningless false imagining, and contemplates the self-nature of all natures. The bodhisattva-mahasattva thus rightly contemplates the nature of external things as without self-nature; this is called the bodhisattva-mahasattva's right contemplation of the nature of external things as without self-nature. How does the bodhisattva-mahasattva rightly be free of the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing? It is that, as all natures are like illusion and dream, both self and other are of a nature that is unarisen, because following the boundary of his own mind-presents. Seeing that external nature is without self-nature, seeing that consciousness is unarisen and that conditions do not heap together, seeing the conditions of imagining, in all the dharmas within and beyond the three realms nothing is obtainable. Seeing freedom from self-nature, the views of arising are all extinguished; knowing that the self-nature of dharmas such as illusion, he attains the acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. Having attained the acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, being free of the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing, this is called the bodhisattva-mahasattva's right discrimination and freedom from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing. How does the bodhisattva-mahasattva attain the joy of self-realized noble wisdom? It is that, having attained the acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, he dwells in the eighth bodhisattva stage. Having attained freedom from the mind, the will, and consciousness, the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the marks of the two selflessnesses, he attains the mind-made body."
World-Honored One! The mind-made body — through what cause?"

The Buddha told Mahamati: "The mind-made [body] is like the going of the mind: swift and unobstructed, hence it is called mind-made. For example, the mind going through stone walls without impediment; in that other direction, for immeasurable yojanas, by reason of what was formerly seen, remembering without forgetting, the mind's own flow never ceasing, in the body there is no obstruction to its arising. Mahamati! Such a mind-made body is attained all at once. The bodhisattva-mahasattva's mind-made body, by the power of the illusion-like samadhi and sovereign transcendent power, adorned with wondrous marks, a body of the sage-class, arises all at once. Like the mind-made, without obstruction, following the primal vow of what he recalls and remembers in his realm, in order to ripen beings, he attains the joy of self-realized noble wisdom. Thus the bodhisattva-mahasattva, having attained the acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, dwelling in the eighth bodhisattva stage, having turned away from and abandoned the body of the mind, the will, and consciousness, the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the marks of the two selflessnesses, and having attained the mind-made body, attains the joy of self-realized noble wisdom. This is called the bodhisattva-mahasattva's accomplishment of the four dharmas through which he attains the great skillful means of the cultivator. One should learn it thus."

Then Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva again requested the World-Honored One: "May [the Buddha] be pleased to teach us the marks of the conditions and causes of all dharmas, so that, having awakened to the marks of conditions and causes, I and the other bodhisattvas may be free of all natures and of the false views of existence and nonexistence; without the false views of imagining, [both] the gradual and the simultaneous arise together."

The Buddha told Mahamati: "All dharmas have two kinds of marks of conditions, namely the external and the internal. The external conditions are: the conditions of skillful means such as clay, a lump, a pillar, a wheel, a rope, water, wood, and human effort, from which a jar is produced. As with a clay jar, so with thread and cloth, grass and a mat, a seed and a sprout, curds and butter; produced by the conditions of skillful means, they are likewise. This is called the external conditions' successive generation. What are the internal conditions? It is that dharmas such as ignorance, craving, and action get the name of "conditions," and from them arise the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and entrances, which get the name of "arisen from conditions." In those there is no difference, yet the foolish imagine. This is called the dharmas of internal conditions. Mahamati! As to causes, there are six kinds, namely: the cause of what is to be, the cause of continuity, the cause of mark, the cause of making, the cause of manifestation, and the cause of dependence. The cause of what is to be: having made the cause, the inner and outer dharmas arise. The cause of continuity: having made the object-support, the inner and outer dharmas arise, the seeds of the aggregates and the rest. The cause of mark: making the mark of immediacy, the continuous [arising] takes place. The cause of making: making the predominating matter, as the wheel-turning king [makes his realm]. The cause of manifestation: when the imagined matter has arisen, the mark is displayed as what is done, as a lamp illuminates forms and then [makes them visible]. The cause of dependence: at the time of cessation it makes the continuity break, and the non-imagined nature arises. Mahamati! Those foolish in their own imagined marks do not arise gradually nor simultaneously. Why? If they arose simultaneously, then what is done and the doer would be without distinction, and the cause-marks would not be obtained. If they arose gradually, the mark of self would not be obtained. What arises gradually does not arise, just as one who has not begotten a son has no name as "father." Mahamati! The gradual successive generation of continuity is not [real], it is only imagining. Because what is born of the conditions of object-support, immediacy, predominance, and the rest [is imagined]. Mahamati! What arises gradually does not arise, because of the mark of attachment to the imagined self-nature. Both gradual and simultaneous do not arise, because of the enjoyment within the present[ation] of one's own mind. The self-marks and common-marks of external nature are without self-nature. Mahamati! Both gradual and simultaneous do not arise, except the present[ation] of one's own mind; because of not noticing imagining, marks arise. Therefore, the marks of the skillful means of the work of conditions and causes: one should be free of the views of both gradual and simultaneous."
All things are wholly unarisen, and there is also no ceasing by conditions,
within that arising and ceasing, one then gives rise to the thought of conditions and causes.
It is not that one negates ceasing and again [there is] arising; the continuous conditions and causes arise,
only in order to break the ordinary fools' deluded imagining of conditions.
The dharmas of conditions and causes, existence and nonexistence — these all are wholly unarisen,
by habitual tendencies deluded and turning, from these the three existences appear.
The condition of true non-arising, also it has no ceasing,
contemplate all the conditioned, like flowers in the sky.
What is grasped and the grasper, relinquish the views of confusion,
not [that which is] already born or about to be born, nor is there [really] a condition or cause.
All things have nothing at all; these are all only speech."
Then Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva again said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One! May [the Buddha] be pleased to speak the sutra of the heart of the marks of speech and imagining.
this is the same as the Buddha-word heart above

World-Honored One! If I and the other bodhisattvas-mahasattvas rightly know the sutra of the heart of the marks of speech and imagining, we will then be able to penetrate the two meanings of speech and the spoken, and quickly attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, so that with the two trends of speech and the spoken we may purify all beings."
The Buddha told Mahamati: "Listen, listen! Think of it well in mind; I will speak it for you."
Mahamati said to the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One! I will gladly receive the teaching."

The Buddha told Mahamati: "There are four kinds of the marks of speech and imagining, namely: the speech of marks, the speech of dreams, the speech of the imagining that attaches to past [things], and the speech of the imagining of beginninglessness. The speech of marks arises from the attachment to the marks of form in one's own imagining. The speech of dreams arises from the recollection of the realm formerly experienced, and arises from the nature of the realm that is without self-nature after awakening. The speech of the imagining that attaches to past [things] arises from the recollection of the deeds done by former enemies. The speech of the imagining of beginninglessness arises from the habitual tendencies of the fault of beginningless false attachment. These are called the four kinds of marks of speech and imagining."

Then Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva, again with this meaning, urged the World-Honored One: "May [the Buddha] be pleased further to speak the realm manifested by speech and imagining. World-Honored One! Where, why, how, and through what cause, do beings' imagining and speech arise?"
The Buddha told Mahamati: "The head, chest, throat, nose, lips, tongue, gums, and teeth, joined together, produce sound."
Mahamati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One! Are speech and imagining the same or not the same?"

The Buddha told Mahamati: "Speech and imagining are neither the same nor not the same. Why? Because there is the mark of its arising from causes. Mahamati! If speech and imagining were different, imagining should not be the cause. If they were not different, then words would not reveal meaning, yet words do reveal [it]. Therefore they are neither the same nor not the same."
Mahamati again said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One! Is speech itself the ultimate truth, or is the thing spoken the ultimate truth?"

The Buddha told Mahamati: "It is not that speech is the ultimate truth, nor is the spoken the ultimate truth. Why? Because that into which the noble bliss of speech enters is the ultimate truth; it is not that speech is the ultimate truth. The ultimate truth is what is attained by the self-realization of noble wisdom; it is not the realm of the awareness of speech and imagining. Therefore speech and imagining do not reveal the ultimate truth. Speech arises from arising and ceasing, movement, and successive conditions. If it arises from successive conditions, it does not reveal the ultimate truth. Mahamati! Because self and other marks are without self-nature, the marks of speech do not reveal the ultimate truth. Moreover, Mahamati! Following the presented measure of one's own mind, the many marks of external nature are without self-nature; speech and imagining do not reveal the ultimate truth. Therefore, Mahamati! One should be free of speech and of all the marks of imagining."
The natures are without self-nature, and likewise there is no speech,
the profound meaning of emptiness of emptiness the foolish cannot know.
The self-nature of all natures, the Dharma of speech is like a shadow,
the son of self-realized noble wisdom — reality is what I have spoken."

Then Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva again said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One! May [the Buddha] be pleased to speak of being free of one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal — what no sectarian practices, what self-realized noble wisdom practices; free of the imagining of self-marks and common-marks, entering into the meaning of the first true reality. The successive signs of the stages, gradually advancing stage upon stage, increasing and purifying, following into the marks of the Tathagata-stage, the primal vow with no development. Like the jewel of many colors, the realm of the measureless marks of practice, the marks of the separate portions presented in one's own mind, all dharmas. May I and the other bodhisattvas-mahasattvas, being free of such imagining of the self-nature's self-marks and common-marks, quickly attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and bring all beings to complete peace and happiness, fully replete."
The Buddha told Mahamati: "Excellent, excellent! You are able to ask me this meaning, [bringing] much peace, much benefit, and compassion for all the gods and people of the world."
