The Buddha told Mahamati: "Listen, listen! Think of it well in mind! I will for you set it forth in discriminating fashion."

The Buddha told Mahamati: "The foolish and ordinary people who do not know the mind-measure grasp the inner and outer natures, relying upon one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal; attached to the self-nature, they cling to imagining from habitual causes. For example, a herd of deer, pressed by thirst, seeing the mirage of springtime, conceive a thought of water, and deluded, run toward it, not knowing it is not water. Thus the foolish, fumigated by beginningless false imagining, with the three poisons burning their hearts, delighting in the realm of forms, seeing arising, abiding, and ceasing, grasp the inner and outer natures, and fall into the thoughts of one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal, grasping through false views. Like a gandharva city, which the ordinary and the foolish, without wisdom, imagine to be a city; [it is] the presentation of the imagination of beginningless habitual tendencies. That is neither a city nor not a city; thus the sectarians, by the attachment of beginningless false habitual tendencies, relying upon the views of one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal, cannot understand the presented measure of their own mind. For example, a person dreaming of men and women, horses and carriages, footsteps, cities, villages, gardens, forests, mountains, rivers, and bathing pools, adorned in all kinds of ways, himself entering within it, and after awakening remembering it. Mahamati! What is your opinion? Is such a person, not relinquishing his recollection of his former dream, a clever one or not?"
Mahamati said to the Buddha: "No, World-Honored One!"

The Buddha told Mahamati: "Thus the ordinary and foolish, devoured by evil views, [possessing] sectarian wisdom, not knowing [things] to be like a dream, the presented measure of their own mind, rely upon the views of one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal. For example, a painted image is neither high nor low, yet the ordinary and foolish form the thought of high and low. Thus, in the future, sectarians filled with the habitual tendencies of evil views, relying upon the views of one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal, ruin themselves and ruin others. The rest, the discourses on freedom from existence and nonexistence and on non-arising, they also say are naught. Slandering the view of cause and effect, they pull up the root of good and destroy the pure cause. The seeker of the highest should go far away from them, saying thus: 'They, falling into the views of self, other, and both, into the imagining of existence and nonexistence, fall into establishment and slander. Through these evil views they will fall into hell.' For example, one with film over his eyes sees hairs floating [in the air], and says to the crowd: 'You all look at this — these are indeed hairs, in the end they are neither a nature nor without nature, because of seeing and not seeing.' Thus the sectarians, with false views and hopes, relying upon the views of one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal, slander the right Dharma, ruining themselves and ruining others. For example, a fire-wheel is not a wheel, [but] the foolish conceive a thought of a wheel; it is not one possessed of wisdom. Thus the sectarians, with evil views and hopes, relying upon the views of one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and nonexistence, eternal and non-eternal, [see] all natures as arising. For example, a water bubble that resembles a mani jewel; the foolish and young, without wisdom, form the thought of a mani jewel and cling to it, chasing after it. That water bubble is neither a mani jewel nor not a mani jewel, because of taking and not taking. Thus the sectarians, fumigated by the habitual tendencies of evil views and imagining, in what is without anything, say there is arising; in what is with conditions, say there is extinction.

Moreover, Mahamati! There are three measures and the five-part treatise; having each established them, one attains the self-realization of noble wisdom. Being free of the matter of the two self-natures, one yet makes the imagining of a nature as existent. Mahamati! When the mind, the will, and consciousness, the body and mind, turn and change, in the presented measure of one's own mind's grasping and grasped, all the imagings are cut off. The cultivator of the Tathagata-stage's self-realized noble wisdom should not, in regard to those, form the thought of nature or non-nature. If again a cultivator, in such a realm, gives rise to the thought of grasping nature or non-nature, he then takes to upholding [views], and takes self and person. Mahamati! If one speaks of the self-nature's self-marks and common-marks, all these are spoken by the transformation Buddha, not by the Dharma Buddha. Moreover, all speech arises from the hopes and views of the ordinary and the foolish; it is not set forth for the sake of the discriminative, partial establishment of the nature of the self-nature's Dharma, nor for the sake of displaying to one who has attained the bliss of the self-realization of noble wisdom's samadhi. For example, in water there is the manifest image of a tree; it is neither an image nor not an image, neither the tree-form nor not the tree-form. Thus the sectarians, fumigated by their views and habits, imagining and clinging, relying upon the views of one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal, are unable to know the presented measure of their own mind. For example, a bright mirror, following conditions, displays all forms and images, yet without imagining. It is neither an image nor not an image, yet one sees image and non-image. The imagining and the foolish form the thought of image. Thus the sectarians' evil views, the images presented of their own mind, imagining and clinging, rely upon the views of one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal. For example, wind and water joined together produce sound; it is neither a nature nor without a nature. Thus the sectarians' evil views and imagining rely upon the views of one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal. For example, the great earth in a place without grass and trees: the hot mirage streams along, great waves of clouds rise up. It is neither a nature nor without a nature, because of greed and non-greed. Thus the ordinary and foolish, fumigated by beginningless false habitual tendencies, imagining and clinging, relying upon arising, abiding, and ceasing, one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal, the gate of the matter in which conditions dwell — they likewise are like that hot mirage and wave. For example, a person set in motion by a mantra and a mechanism: by the pishacha ghosts, which are not of the number of living beings, conjointly brought about, shaking and moving, speaking and acting. The ordinary and the foolish imagine and cling to going and coming. Thus the sectarians, with evil views and hopes, relying upon the views of one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal, cling to idle discourse and establish what is unreal. Mahamati! Therefore, wishing to attain the matter of self-realized noble wisdom, one should be free of the evil views and imagining of arising, abiding, and ceasing, one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal, and the rest."
Illusion, dream, the tree-image in water, floating hairs, the springtime mirage,
thus contemplating the three existences, one finally attains liberation.
For example, the deer's thirst-thought, moving and deluding the mind,
the deer think it is water, yet in truth there is no water.
Thus the seeds of consciousness, moving, see the realm,
the ordinary foolish imagining arises, as one is veiled by the film [on the eye].
In beginningless birth-and-death, clinging to the nature that is grasped,
like [?] emerging
, relinquishing the grasping of greed,
like illusion, mantra, and mechanism, floating clouds, dream, and lightning.
Contemplating this, one attains liberation, forever cutting off the three continuities;
in that there is nothing made, like a mirage or the sky.
Thus knowing all dharmas, one is then [one who] knows nothing,
the teachings are only provisional names, and those too have no mark.
In that, giving rise to imagining, the aggregates and processes are like floating hairs,
like a painting, floating hairs, and illusion, dream, and a gandharva city.
The fire-wheel, the springtime mirage: nonexistent, yet appearing to beings,
eternal and non-eternal, one and different, both and neither, likewise.
The continuity of beginningless faults, the ordinary and foolish [in] deluded imagining,
a bright mirror, water, the pure eye, the mani precious jewel,
within it all forms appear, yet in truth nothing at all [is there].
All natures are manifested, like a painting or the springtime mirage,
all manner of forms appear, like a dream, with nothing at all [there].

Moreover, Mahamati! The Tathagata's teaching of the Dharma is free of these four phrases, namely: one and different, both and neither, existence and nonexistence, existence and non-existence, eternal and non-eternal. Free of the discriminative establishment and slander of existence and nonexistence. Gathering together the true meaning, dependent-arising, the Way and its cessation, and liberation — with these as the foremost, the Tathagata teaches the Dharma. It is not self-nature, not sovereignty, not absence of cause, not atoms, not time, not the continuous self-nature, [by which] he teaches the Dharma. Moreover, Mahamati! To purify the hindrance of the defilements and of the knowable, for example, like a caravan-leader, he successively establishes the hundred-and-eight phrases as without anything, and rightly discriminates the various vehicles and the marks of the stages."

Moreover, Mahamati, there are four kinds of dhyana. What are the four? They are: the dhyana practiced by the ignorant, the dhyana that examines meaning, the dhyana that is yoked to suchness, and the Tathagata dhyana. What is the dhyana practiced by the ignorant? It is this: the shravakas, the pratyekabuddhas and the practitioners of the externalist paths contemplate the selflessness of persons; they take the self-marks and common marks, the chain of bones, and the marks of impermanence, suffering and impurity as their chief concern. Thus they contemplate these marks without distinction, advancing from one to the next, and their notions are neither removed nor destroyed — this is called the dhyana practiced by the ignorant. What is the dhyana that examines meaning? It is this: having understood the self-marks and common marks of the selflessness of persons, and that for the externalists both self and other are without nature, one contemplates the selflessness of dharmas and the meaning of the marks of that level, advancing by stages — this is called the dhyana that examines meaning. What is the dhyana that is yoked to suchness? It is this: in the imagining of the two kinds of selflessness, no imagining arises in the place of suchness — this is called the dhyana that is yoked to suchness. What is the Tathagata dhyana? It is this: entering the Tathagata ground, walking in the marks of self-realized noble wisdom and the three kinds of blissful abiding, and accomplishing for beings what is inconceivable — this is called the Tathagata dhyana.”
The dhyana of the common fold, the dhyana that examines meaning’s marks,
the dhyana turned to suchness, the Tathagata’s dhyana pure.
As the sun and the moon, as the blue lotus in the deep ravine,
as empty space and dying embers — thus the practitioner observes.
Thus do the various marks and the dhyanas of the externalist paths
also fall to the shravakas and to the realm of the pratyekabuddhas.
Abandoning all of these, one arrives at nothing whatsoever.
All the Buddhas of every land, with their inconceivable hands,
at one time stroke his head, and he enters the marks of suchness.”
At that time Mahamati the great bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as to nirvana, of what dharma is it spoken, that it is called nirvana?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “The habit-energy of all self-natures, and the transformation of the habit-energy and views of the storehouse consciousness — this is called nirvana. The nirvana of all the Buddhas and of myself is the realm of the emptiness of self-nature.

Moreover, Mahamati, nirvana is the realm of the noble wisdom that is self-realized, free from the imaginings of annihilation and permanence, of nature and non-nature. How is it not permanent? Because the imaginings of self-marks and common marks are cut off, therefore it is not permanent. How is it not annihilated? Because all the noble ones of the past, future and present attain self-realization, therefore it is not annihilated. Mahamati, nirvana is neither destroyed nor does it die. If nirvana were death, there would again be rebirth and a continuing stream. If it were destruction, it would fall into the marks of the conditioned. Therefore nirvana is free from destruction and free from death. Therefore it is the refuge of practitioners.
Moreover, Mahamati, nirvana is neither renunciation nor attainment, neither annihilation nor permanence, neither one meaning nor various meanings. This is called nirvana.

Moreover, Mahamati, as for the nirvana of the shravakas and pratyekabuddhas: they awaken to self-marks and common marks, they do not habituate themselves to sense-objects, their views are not inverted, and imaginings do not arise. They, in that, make the awakening called nirvana.

Moreover, Mahamati, there are two kinds of marks of self-nature. What are the two? They are: the grasping at the mark of the self-nature of words, and the grasping at the mark of the self-nature of things. As for grasping at the mark of the self-nature of words, it arises from grasping at the habit-energy of the falsehood of beginningless words. As for grasping at the mark of the self-nature of things, it arises from not awakening to the boundaries of what is manifested by one’s own mind.

Moreover, Mahamati, the Tathagata establishes by two kinds of spiritual power, and the great bodhisattvas bow in homage to all the Buddhas, listen, receive and question the meaning. What are the two kinds of spiritual power by which he establishes them? They are: the spiritual power of the true reception of samadhi, which manifests all bodies, faces and words, and the spiritual power of the hand that confers consecration. Mahamati, the great bodhisattva, at the first bodhisattva ground, dwells in the Buddha’s spiritual power — that is to say, he enters the bodhisattva great-vehicle illumination samadhi. Having entered this samadhi, all the Buddhas of the ten quarters, by their spiritual power, manifest all bodies, faces and words for him, as for the great bodhisattva Vajragarbha and for the other great bodhisattvas who have accomplished merits of that kind. Mahamati, this is called the first bodhisattva ground. When the great bodhisattva has obtained the spiritual power of the true reception of the bodhisattva samadhi — accomplished by the accumulation of roots of goodness through a hundred thousand kalpas — he passes through the marks of the grounds in order, and of the remedies and what is to be remedied, penetrating to the end, until he reaches the Cloud of Dharma ground; there he dwells in a subtle and wonderful palace of the great lotus, seated on a jewel lion throne within the great lotus, surrounded by a retinue of great bodhisattvas of his own kind, his body adorned with strings of many jewels, like gold, saffron, the sun and the moon in brightness. The hands of the most victorious ones come from the ten quarters, and as he sits on the seat in the palace of the great lotus they confer consecration upon his head. Just as a wheel-turning sage king who is sovereign in himself, or the crown prince of Indra, king of the gods, is consecrated — this is called the spiritual power of the bodhisattva’s hand consecration. Mahamati, these are called the two kinds of spiritual power of the great bodhisattva. If the great bodhisattva dwells in the two kinds of spiritual power, he sees the Tathagatas face to face; if not thus, he cannot see them. Moreover, Mahamati, whatever the great bodhisattva discriminates regarding samadhi, the bases of spiritual power, and the practice of teaching the Dharma, all of it dwells in the Tathagata’s two kinds of spiritual power. Mahamati, if the great bodhisattva, apart from the Buddha’s spiritual power, could expound and speak, then all ordinary beings too should be able to speak. Why is that? Because they do not dwell in spiritual power. Mahamati, the mountains, rocks, trees, and all musical instruments, city walls and palaces, by the power of the Tathagata’s majesty when he enters the city, all of themselves give forth the sound of music — how much more so those that have a mind. The deaf, the blind, the mute, and beings in measureless sufferings all obtain liberation. The Tathagata has such measureless spiritual powers as these to benefit and pacify living beings.”

Mahamati the bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, for what reason does the Tathagata, the worthy one, the fully enlightened one, add his spiritual power when the great bodhisattva dwells in the true reception of samadhi, and when he is consecrated on the higher advancing grounds?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “It is in order that they may be free from the karma of Mara and from afflictions, and may not fall into the dhyana of the shravaka grounds; and in order that they may attain the Tathagata’s ground of self-realization, and increase the Dharma they have obtained. Therefore the Tathagata, the worthy one, the fully enlightened one, establishes all great bodhisattvas by his spiritual power. If he did not establish them by spiritual power, they would fall into the evil views and imaginings of the externalists, and into the expectations of the shravakas and the hosts of Mara, and would not attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. For this reason all the Buddhas and Tathagatas embrace and receive all great bodhisattvas by their spiritual power.”
The honored one among men, by spiritual power, with all his great vows made pure,
in samadhi confers consecration, on the first ground and the tenth.”

At that time Mahamati the great bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, the Buddha speaks of dependent origination, speaking thus of causes and conditions, yet he does not speak of the one who creates. World-Honored One, the externalists also speak of causes and conditions — saying that they arise from Ishvara, from the self, from time, from atoms — and thus the various natures arise. But when the World-Honored One speaks of the various natures arising from causes and conditions, that is what is spoken of as the siddhanta of the expressible and the siddhanta of the inexpressible
siddhanta is rendered in meaning as ‘tenet’ by some, as ‘accomplishment’ by others, and as ‘setting aside’ by others

. World-Honored One, the externalists also speak of production from being and non-being, and the World-Honored One also speaks of production from non-being, that having arisen it ceases. As when the World-Honored One says: ‘Ignorance conditions the formations, and so on up to old age and death’ — this is the World-Honored One’s teaching of no cause, not the teaching of a cause. The World-Honored One establishes and speaks thus: ‘This being, that becomes’ — he does not establish a gradual production. And one observes that the externalists’ teaching is superior, and not the Tathagata’s. Why is that? World-Honored One, the externalists say that a cause produces what is produced without arising from conditions. The World-Honored One says that when a cause is observed there is an effect, and when an effect is observed there is a cause. Thus causes and conditions are confused, and thus they proceed endlessly, one after another.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “I do not teach without a cause, nor do I teach that causes and conditions are confused. When I say ‘This being, that becomes,’ it means that the grasping and the grasped are without nature, and that one awakens to the measure of what is manifested by one’s own mind. Mahamati, if one grasps at grasping and the grasped, not awakening to the measure of what is manifested by one’s own mind, then the natures of external objects are taken as nature and non-nature, and such a one has that fault; it is not my teaching of dependent origination. I always say: ‘Dharmas arise from the convergence of causes and conditions,’ not that they arise without a cause.”

Mahamati again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, is it not that words have a nature, and that there is a nature in all things? World-Honored One, if there were no nature, words would not arise. World-Honored One, therefore words have a nature, and there is a nature in all things.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “Words are made about what is without nature — as with the horns of a rabbit and the hair of a turtle, and the like, which are spoken of in the world. Mahamati, they are neither nature nor non-nature; they are words only. If, as you say, the self-nature of words meant that there is a nature in all things, then your thesis is destroyed. Mahamati, it is not that every land has words. Words are but a mark of making. In some Buddha lands, a gaze reveals the Dharma; in others, a making of marks, or the raising of the eyebrows, or the moving of the eyes, or a smile, or a yawn, or a cough, or recollection of a land, or a shaking of the body. Mahamati, as with the gaze, so in the world of Fragrance Accumulation, the land of the Tathagata Universal Worthy, by a gaze alone the bodhisattvas obtain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, and the supreme samadhi. Therefore it is not that words have a nature, or that there is a nature in all things. Mahamati, look at the mosquitoes, gnats, ants and the like in this world: these beings have no words, and yet each accomplishes its work.”
As empty space, as a rabbit’s horn, and as the child of a barren woman,
so what is not, yet is spoken of — such is the imagining of nature.
Dharmas that are causes and conditions conjoined, the common and foolish raise imaginings;
unable to know them as they really are, they turn about in the house of the three realms.”
At that time Mahamati the great bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as to the word ‘permanent,’ of what matter is it spoken?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “It is spoken of delusion. For by that delusion the noble ones too are manifested, yet they are not inverted. Mahamati, it is like the heat haze in spring, the wheel of fire, the hanging hair, the city of the gandharvas, illusions, dreams, and mirror images. The world is inverted, but it is not the wise; yet they are not unmanifested. Mahamati, that delusion has various manifestations, and it is not that delusion makes impermanence. Why is that? Because it is free from nature and non-nature. Mahamati, what is the delusion that is free from nature and non-nature? It is the various objects of all foolish ordinary beings. It is like the Ganges river, which hungry ghosts do not see and others do see: thus it has no nature of delusion; yet because it is manifested to others, it is not without nature. Thus delusion is, for the noble ones, free from the inverted and the non-inverted. Therefore delusion is permanent, because the mark of marks is not destroyed. Mahamati, it is not that the various marks and imagined marks of delusion are destroyed; therefore delusion is permanent. Mahamati, how is delusion real? If, again, for causes and conditions, the noble ones, in this delusion, do not give rise to the awakening that is inverted, nor to the awakening that is non-inverted. Mahamati, apart from the noble ones, as to this delusion there is a little thought in it, which is not a thought of the business of noble wisdom.

Mahamati, whatever has being is the foolish ordinary beings’ false speech, not the speech of the noble ones. As for that delusion: the imaginings of the inverted and the non-inverted give rise to two kinds of lineage — namely, the lineage of the noble ones and the lineage of the foolish ordinary beings. The lineage of the noble ones has three distinctions: the shravaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Buddha vehicle. How do the imaginings of the foolish ordinary beings give rise to the lineage of the shravaka vehicle? By grasping at self-marks and common marks, the lineage of the shravaka vehicle arises; this is called the lineage of the shravaka vehicle arising from imagining. Mahamati, from that very deluded imagining the lineage of the pratyekabuddha vehicle arises. That is to say: as to that very delusion’s self-marks and common marks, one does not contemplate or grasp them, and the lineage of the pratyekabuddha vehicle arises. How is it with the wise? From that very deluded imagining the lineage of the Buddha vehicle arises. That is to say: awakening to the measure of what is manifested by one’s own mind, and that external natures are without nature, one does not imagine marks, and the lineage of the Buddha vehicle arises; this is called the lineage of the Buddha vehicle arising from that very delusion. Moreover, as to the nature of various things, the deluded imaginings of ordinary beings give rise to the lineage of the foolish ordinary beings. These are neither a thing nor no thing; this is the meaning of lineage. Mahamati, when one does not imagine that very delusion, and the self-nature of the dharmas of the habit-energy and faults of the mind, mentation and consciousness of the noble ones is transformed, this is called suchness. Therefore it is said that suchness is apart from mind. I speak this phrase to reveal freedom from imagining, that is, to speak of freedom from all imagining.”
Mahamati addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, is delusion a thing or no thing?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “It is like an illusion, without the mark of grasping. If delusion had the mark of grasping, then the nature of grasping could not be destroyed, and dependent origination would be as the externalists say, who teach that dharmas arise from causes and conditions.”
Mahamati addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if delusion is like an illusion, it would again be a cause for further delusion.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “It is not that an illusion is a cause of delusion, for it gives rise to no fault. Mahamati, an illusion gives rise to no fault, and has no imagining. Mahamati, an illusion arises from another’s place of clarity; it does not arise from the place of one’s own imagined habit-energy. Therefore it gives rise to no fault. Mahamati, this is the deluded grasping of the foolish mind, and not of the noble and wise.”
The noble ones do not see delusion; in the middle, too, there is nothing real.
If the middle were real, then delusion itself would be real.
If, all delusion abandoned, a mark should yet arise,
that too is delusion, impure as a film upon the eye.
Moreover, Mahamati, apart from illusion there is nothing that resembles it; see all dharmas as an illusion.”

Mahamati addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, is it by grasping at various illusory marks that you say all dharmas are like an illusion? Or by grasping at other marks? If, by grasping at various illusory marks, you say that all natures are like an illusion, then, World-Honored One, there are natures that are not like an illusion. Why is that? Because the various marks of form are not a cause. World-Honored One, there is no cause by which the various marks of form appear like an illusion. World-Honored One, therefore it is not that the grasping at various illusory marks is a likeness of nature, so that all is like an illusion.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “It is not by grasping at the likeness of various illusory marks that all dharmas are like an illusion. Mahamati, it is because all dharmas are unreal and perish swiftly like lightning that they are like an illusion. Mahamati, it is like a flash of lightning: it appears for the space of an instant, and having appeared is immediately destroyed, and is not manifested to foolish ordinary beings. Thus all natures — one’s own imagined self-marks and common marks — are observed to be without nature; it is not by grasping at the marks of manifested form.”
No simile can match illusion, and so the Dharma’s nature is taught as illusion;
unreal, swift as lightning — therefore it is called illusion.”

Mahamati again addressed the Buddha, saying: “As the World-Honored One has said, all natures are unborn, and also like an illusion: is not the World-Honored One’s earlier and later teaching self-contradictory — speaking of the nature of the unborn as like an illusion?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “It is not that my teaching of the nature of the unborn as like an illusion is the fault of earlier and later contradiction. Why is that? Because birth and non-birth are the measure of what is manifested by one’s own mind; being and non-being, and external natures as without nature, are the manifestation of the unborn. Mahamati, it is not that I have the fault of earlier and later contradiction in my teaching. But in order to destroy the externalists’ production from a cause, I teach that all natures are unborn. Mahamati, the externalists are a mass of delusion; they wish to make being and non-being arise, and not from the conditions of their own various imagined graspings. Mahamati, I do not teach that being and non-being arise; therefore I teach by way of the teaching of the unborn. Mahamati, when I speak of natures, it is in order to embrace birth and death, to destroy the views of nihilism and annihilationism, and because my disciples embrace the various actions and the places of rebirth; therefore with the word ‘nature’ I speak, embracing birth and death. Mahamati, when I speak of the marks of the self-nature of illusion, it is in order to be free from the marks of the self-nature of nature, and from the expectations of the marks of the evil views of foolish ordinary beings who do not know the measure of what is manifested by their own minds. To destroy production wrought by a cause, and grasping at the marks of the self-nature of conditions, I speak of the self-nature and marks of illusion and dream in all dharmas, so that foolish ordinary beings may not, by the expectations of evil views, grasp at all dharmas, their own and others’, and see them in the place of suchness, and so make a false treatise. Mahamati, to see all dharmas in the place of suchness is to awaken to the measure of what is manifested by one’s own mind.”
The unborn is made out to be without nature; nature embraces birth and death.
One observes all as like an illusion, and does not imagine marks.

Moreover, Mahamati, I shall now speak of the marks of names, sentences and forms. The great bodhisattva who well observes names, sentences and forms follows and enters the meaning and the forms of sentences, and swiftly attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Having thus awakened, he awakens all living beings. Mahamati, as for the name-body: when a name is set up in dependence on a thing, this is called the name-body. As for the sentence-body: a sentence has a body of meaning, its self-nature is definitely settled and final — this is called the sentence-body. As for the form-body: that which displays names and sentences is called the form-body
the form-body is the letter

. Moreover, the form-body is long and short, high and low. Moreover, the sentence-body is a path or track: like the tracks walked by elephants, horses, people and beasts, it receives the name of sentence-body. Mahamati, as for name and form: because a name speaks of the four immaterial aggregates, it is called a name; because self-marks are manifested, it is called form. These are called names, sentences and forms. The boundaries of the marks of names, sentences and forms should be learned.”
The name-body and the sentence-body, and the form-body’s distinctions,
the foolish ordinary beings grasp at, as an elephant sunk in deep mud.

Moreover, Mahamati, the wise of future ages should question the unwise, by the marks of the view that is free from oneness and difference, and from both and neither, concerning the meaning I have penetrated. They will answer, saying: ‘This is not a proper question.’ They ask whether form and the like are permanent or impermanent, different or not different; and likewise concerning nirvana, the marks of the formations and what is marked, the qualities and what possesses the qualities, the maker and what is made, the seer and what is seen, the atom and the subtle particle, the cultivator and the cultivation — such mutually revolving marks as these. When such questions are asked, they say that the Buddha taught the unrecorded and the setting aside of discussion. This is not something the deluded can know, because the wisdom of hearing is not complete in them. The Tathagata, the worthy one, the fully enlightened one, in order to free them from words of terror, speaks of the unrecorded and does not make a record for them. And again, to stop the externalists’ views and discussions, he does not speak. Mahamati, the externalists speak thus: ‘The life-principle is the body,’ and such unrecorded teachings. Mahamati, those externalists are foolish; they make unrecorded teachings about a cause, which I do not speak. Mahamati, what I speak is free from grasping and the grasped, and imagining does not arise. How does one stop them? Mahamati, those who grasp at grasping and the grasped do not know the measure of what is manifested by their own minds; therefore one stops them. Mahamati, the Tathagata, the worthy one, the fully enlightened one, teaches beings by the four kinds of record. Mahamati, the setting aside of record I teach from time to time, for those whose faculties are not yet ripe, not for those who are ripe.

Moreover, Mahamati, all dharmas do not arise apart from what is made and from causes and conditions, because there is no maker; therefore all dharmas are unborn. Mahamati, why is every nature free from self-nature? Because when one observes with self-awakening, the marks of self and common are unattainable; therefore it is said that all dharmas are unborn. Why is it that all dharmas cannot be brought here or carried away? Because, as to self-marks and common marks, if one wishes to bring them, there is nothing that comes; if one wishes to carry them away, there is nothing that goes. Therefore all dharmas are free from bringing and carrying away. Mahamati, why do all dharmas not cease? Because the marks of self-nature are absent, and all dharmas are unattainable; therefore all dharmas do not cease. Mahamati, why are all dharmas impermanent? Because marks arise with the nature of impermanence; therefore it is said that all dharmas are impermanent. Mahamati, why are all dharmas permanent? Because marks arise with the nature of the unborn, and impermanence is permanent; therefore it is said that all dharmas are permanent.”
Record and teaching are four in kind: the categorical and the counter-question,
the analytical and the setting aside — by these he governs the externalists.
Those who hold production from being and from non-being, the Samkhya and Vaisheshika teachers,
are all of them unrecorded; thus are they shown forth.
What the fully awakened one discriminates, self-nature, is unattainable;
and because he is free from words, he speaks of being free from self-nature.”

At that time Mahamati the great bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I pray you, speak to us of the stream-enterers and of the marks of the distinctions in the stream-enterer’s course. If the great bodhisattva well understands the marks of the distinctions in the stream-enterer’s course, and the marks of the expedients of the once-returner, the non-returner and the arhat, and having discriminated and known them, teaches the Dharma to living beings in accordance with them — namely, the marks of the two kinds of selflessness and the purification of the two obstructions, and the marks of passing through the grounds, penetrating to the end, and attaining the Tathagatas’ inconceivable and ultimate realm. Like a wishfulfilling jewel of many colors, he is well able to benefit all living beings, and with the inexhaustible body and wealth of the realm of all dharmas he embraces and nourishes them all.”
The Buddha told Mahamati: “Listen well, listen well, and ponder it well in your mind. I shall now speak to you.”
Mahamati addressed the Buddha, saying: “Excellent, World-Honored One; with reverence I receive it.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “There are three kinds of stream-enterers, and distinctions in the fruit of stream-entry. What are the three? They are the lower, the middle and the upper. The lower has at most seven more births; the middle, after three or five more births, enters parinirvana; the upper enters parinirvana in that very birth. These three kinds have three fetters, lower, middle and upper. What are the three fetters? They are the view of the body, doubt, and the grasping at rites. In these distinctions of the three fetters, advancing higher and higher, one attains arhatship. Mahamati, the view of the body is of two kinds: the innate and the imagined. They are like the imagining of dependent origination, and the imagining of self-nature. For example, relying on the self-nature of dependent origination, the various imagined self-natures arise through grasping. Because these are neither existent nor non-existent nor both, they have no real marks of imagining. Foolish ordinary beings imagine, and grasp at the marks of various imagined self-natures, like the heat haze in which deer imagine water. This is the stream-enterer’s imagined view of the body; by embracing selflessness of persons, he destroys the long-standing grasping of unknowing. Mahamati, as for the innate: the stream-enterer’s view of the body holds that his own body and others’ bodies are the four aggregates, because they are without the marks of form. Form arises from the made and the maker, and because of the marks of mutually causing one another, the great elements and form do not accumulate. When the stream-enterer contemplates the views of the divisions of existence and non-existence, the view of the body is cut off. When the view of the body is thus cut off, greed does not arise; these are the marks of the view of the body. Mahamati, as for the marks of doubt: because he has well seen the marks of the Dharma, and because the two former kinds of imagining of the view of the body are cut off, doubt about the Dharma does not arise, and he does not give rise elsewhere to the view of a teacher, as to pure and impure. These are the marks of doubt cut off by the stream-enterer. Mahamati, as for the grasping at rites: how does the stream-enterer not grasp at rites? Because he has well seen the marks of suffering in the places of rebirth, therefore he does not grasp. Mahamati, the grasping is this: foolish ordinary beings, determined to undertake and cultivate austerities, seek rebirth for the sake of the implements of various pleasures; but he does not grasp at these, except when he dedicates himself to the superiority of self-awakening, free from imagining, and undertakes the limbs of the precepts as an expedient for the practice of the marks of the undefiled Dharma. These are the marks of the stream-enterer’s grasping at rites cut off. The stream-enterer cuts off the three fetters, and greed and delusion do not arise. If the stream-enterer should think: ‘These fetters are not accomplished in me,’ there would be two faults: he would fall into the view of the body, and the fetters would not be cut off.”
Mahamati addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, the World-Honored One speaks of many kinds of craving: which craving is it that is cut off?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “The love and attachment that is entangled with women, and the grasping at various expedients, and the evil deeds of body and speech, taking present pleasure and sowing future suffering — these do not arise in him. Why is that? Because he has obtained the joy of the true reception of samadhi. Therefore these are cut off in him; it is not that the craving that tends toward nirvana is cut off. Mahamati, what are the marks of the once-returner? It is this: he instantly illumines the marks of form, the imagining of arising, and the marks of seeing do not arise. Because he has well seen the marks of the course of dhyana, he comes once more to this world, makes an end of suffering, and attains nirvana; therefore he is called a once-returner. Mahamati, what is the non-returner? It is this: as to the marks of form of past, future and present, nature and non-nature, he sees the faults of arising, and does not give rise to imagining, and the fetters are cut off; therefore he is called a non-returner. Mahamati, as for the arhat: it is this — the dhyanas, samadhis, liberations, powers and illuminations, and the afflictions and sufferings whose imaginings are without nature; therefore he is called an arhat.”

Mahamati addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, the World-Honored One speaks of three kinds of arhat. Of which arhat is he speaking? World-Honored One, is it the shravaka who attains the one vehicle of tranquility? Or the great bodhisattva who manifests an arhat by expedient means? Or one conjured by the Buddha?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “It is the shravaka who attains the one vehicle of tranquility, and not the others. The others walk the bodhisattva practice, and are conjured by the Buddha; by the power of their skillful expedients and original vows they manifest birth among the great assembly, to adorn the Buddha’s retinue. Mahamati, in the place of imagining they teach the various dharmas, speaking of the attainment of the fruit and the attainment of dhyana. The dhyana of one who enters dhyana has wholly passed away; so they manifest the attainment of the measure of what is manifested by their own minds, and the marks of the fruit, and this is called the attainment of the fruit. Moreover, Mahamati, one who wishes to go beyond the dhyanas, the four measureless ones, and the formless realms should be free from the marks of the measure manifested by his own mind. Mahamati, it is not so that the true reception of feeling and perception goes beyond the measure of what is manifested by one’s own mind. Why is that? Because there is a measure of mind.”
Dhyana, the four measureless ones, the formless samapattis,
the cessation of all feeling and perception — these are not the measure of mind.
The fruit of stream-entry, the once-returner and the non-returner,
and the arhat as well — all these are the mind’s delusion.
The dhyana of the cultivator, and the conditions of dhyana, cut off and known, are the true truth;
this is the measure of imagining; if one awakens, one is liberated.

Moreover, Mahamati, there are two kinds of awakening: the awakening of observation, and the awakening of the establishing of the grasping at the marks of imagining. Mahamati, the awakening of observation is this: if, as to the awakened marks of the self-nature of nature, one selects and finds them unattainable apart from the four propositions, this is called the awakening of observation. Mahamati, those four propositions are: apart from oneness and difference, both and neither, being and non-being and neither being nor non-being, and permanence and impermanence — these are called the four propositions. Mahamati, apart from these four propositions, this is called all dharmas. Mahamati, one should learn to observe all dharmas by these four propositions. Mahamati, what is the awakening of the establishing of the grasping at the marks of imagining? It is this: the grasping at the marks of imagining, and the grasping at the four great elements as the unreal imagined marks of solidity, moisture, warmth and motion. The grasping at the theses, reasons, examples and inferences, and the establishing of what is not real as real — this is called the awakening of the establishing of the grasping at the marks of imagining. These are called the two kinds of marks of awakening. If the great bodhisattva accomplishes these two marks of awakening, the marks of the selflessness of persons and dharmas are brought to the end, and he well knows the expedient, the awakening of nothing whatsoever. Observing the grounds of practice, he attains the first ground, enters a hundred samadhis, obtains the samadhis of distinction, sees a hundred Buddhas and a hundred bodhisattvas, and knows the affairs of a hundred kalpas before and after; the light illumines a hundred Buddha lands, and he knows the marks of the higher and higher grounds, with great vows, supreme spiritual powers and sovereignty. Consecrated by the Cloud of Dharma, he shall attain the Tathagata’s ground of self-awakening, well binding his mind to the ten inexhaustible phrases, maturing living beings, with various transformations, adorned with radiance, because he obtains the true reception of the samadhi of the noble bliss of self-awakening.

Moreover, Mahamati, the great bodhisattva should be well skilled in the four great elements and the form they produce. How is the great bodhisattva well skilled in the four great elements and the form they produce? Mahamati, the great bodhisattva learns thus: for one who sees the ultimate truth, the four great elements are unborn. As to the non-arising of the four great elements, he makes such an observation. Having observed, he awakens to the boundaries of the imagining of names and marks, and to the boundaries of what is manifested by his own mind, and that external natures are without nature; this is called the boundary of the imagining of what is manifested by one’s own mind. That is to say: observing the three realms, the nature of the four great elements and the form they produce is apart, the four propositions are penetrated and purified, and he is free from self and what belongs to self. Dwelling in the boundaries of the marks of suchness and of self-marks, the self-mark of the unborn is accomplished. Mahamati, how do those four great elements produce form? It is this: the imagined great element of moisture produces the inner and outer realm of water; the imagined great element of capability produces the inner and outer realm of fire; the imagined great element of motion produces the inner and outer realm of wind; the imagined great element of the severed mark of form produces the inner and outer realm of earth. Form and space together, the grasping at false truths, the accumulation of the five aggregates, and the four great elements produce form. Mahamati, as for consciousness: because it delights in the objects of various tracks, it continues in the other destinies. Mahamati, earth and the other four great elements, and the form they produce, have the four great elements as their condition, and are not the condition of those four great elements. Why is that? Because the expedients wrought as to the marks of nature and form are without nature, and the great elements do not arise. Mahamati, the expedients wrought as to the marks of nature and form arise in conjunction, and are not without form. Therefore the marks of the four great elements and the form they produce are the imagining of the externalists, and not mine.

Moreover, Mahamati, I shall now speak of the marks of the self-nature of the aggregates. What are the marks of the self-nature of the aggregates? They are the five aggregates. What are the five? They are form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. The four aggregates are not form: they are feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. Mahamati, as for form: it is the four great elements and the form they produce, each with its own distinct marks. Mahamati, formless things are not four in number, like empty space. For example, empty space transcends the marks of number and is free from number, yet imagining speaks of it as one empty space. Mahamati, thus the aggregates transcend the marks of number and are free from number, free from nature and non-nature, free from the four propositions. The marks of number are the speech of foolish ordinary beings, and what they speak is not that of the noble and wise. Mahamati, the noble ones, like an illusion, manifest various forms and images, free from the postulation of difference and non-difference. And again, like a man in a dream or a shadow, they are free from difference and non-difference. Mahamati, the course of noble wisdom is manifested in the same way as the imagining of the aggregates. These are called the marks of the self-nature of the aggregates. You should remove and destroy them; having destroyed them, speak the Dharma of tranquility, and cut off the views of all the externalists in every Buddha land. Mahamati, when one speaks of tranquility, the view of the selflessness of dharmas is purified, and one enters the ground of immovability. Having entered the ground of immovability, one has sovereignty in measureless samadhis, and obtains the body born of will, and obtains the samadhi of illusion, penetrating to the end, with sovereignty in powers and illuminations, saving, embracing and benefiting all living beings — as the great earth bears and nourishes living beings. The great bodhisattva who ferries all living beings across is likewise thus.

Moreover, Mahamati, the externalists have four kinds of nirvana. What are the four? They are: the nirvana in which the self-nature of nature is without nature; the nirvana in which the natures of various marks are without nature; the nirvana of awakening to the self-marks and self-nature as without nature; and the nirvana in which the self-marks and common marks of the aggregates, and their continuing stream, are cut off. These are called the four kinds of nirvana of the externalists, which are not the dharma I speak. Mahamati, what I speak is this: when the imagining consciousness ceases, this is called nirvana.”
Mahamati addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, is the eightfold consciousness not established?”
The Buddha said: “It is established.”
Mahamati addressed the Buddha, saying: “If it is established, why is it that consciousness is left behind, and not the seven consciousnesses?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “Because of that cause and that support, the seven consciousnesses do not arise. As for consciousness: the habit-energy born of grasping at the segments of objects nourishes the storehouse consciousness together with mentation. The grasping at self and what belongs to self, and the causes and conditions of thought, arise. The storehouse consciousness of the indestructible marks of the body, by depending on and supporting the objects manifested by its own mind, gives rise to the mass of the grasping mind, and they cause one another in turn. It is like the waves of the sea, stirred by the wind of the objects manifested by one’s own mind, arising and ceasing; thus it is also. Therefore when consciousness ceases, the seven consciousnesses also cease.”
I do not take nirvana to be a nature, nor what is made, nor its marks;
when the imagining consciousness of objects ceases, that for me is nirvana.
By that cause and that support, and by the aims and the like, the body is formed;
that which is the cause is the mind, and it is the support of the consciousnesses.
As when the great current of water is exhausted, the waves no longer rise,
so when consciousness ceases, the various consciousnesses do not arise.

Moreover, Mahamati, I shall now speak of the marks of the distinctions of the self-nature of imagining. If one well discriminates the marks of the distinctions of the self-nature of imagining, then you and the other great bodhisattvas will be free from imagining, reach the noble self-awakening, well see the courses of the externalists, and awaken to the grasping and the grasped, so that imagining is cut off. The various marks of dependent origination and the course of the self-nature of imagining will no longer be imagined. Mahamati, what are the marks of the distinctions of the self-nature of imagining? They are: the imagining of words, the imagining of the things spoken of, the imagining of marks, the imagining of gain, the imagining of self-nature, the imagining of cause, the imagining of views, the imagining of accomplishment, the imagining of birth, the imagining of non-birth, the imagining of continuity, and the imagining of bondage and non-bondage. These are called the marks of the distinctions of the self-nature of imagining. Mahamati, what is the imagining of words? It is this: the grasping at the pleasing delight of various lovely sounds, songs and voices — this is called the imagining of words. Mahamati, what is the imagining of the things spoken of? It is this: there is a self-nature of the things spoken of, known by noble wisdom, and depending on that, the imagining of words arises. This is called the imagining of the things spoken of. Mahamati, what is the imagining of marks? It is this: as to those very things spoken of, like the deer’s imagining of water, one grasps at them with various graspings. That is to say: the marks of solidity, moisture, warmth and motion, and the imagining of all natures. This is called the imagining of marks. Mahamati, what is the imagining of gain? It is this: delight in various golds, silvers and precious treasures. This is called the imagining of gain. Mahamati, what is the imagining of self-nature? It is this: that self-nature holds this to be so, not different — the imagining of evil views. This is called the imagining of self-nature. Mahamati, what is the imagining of cause? It is this: whether cause or condition, being and non-being are discriminated, and the mark of cause arises. This is called the imagining of cause. Mahamati, what is the imagining of views? It is this: the evil views of being and non-being, oneness and difference, both and neither, and the grasping at the imaginings of the externalists. This is called the imagining of views. Mahamati, what is the imagining of accomplishment? It is this: the notions of self and what belongs to self, accomplished as a definite thesis. This is called the imagining of accomplishment.

Mahamati, what is the imagining of birth? It is this: grasping at the production of being and non-being from nature. This is called the imagining of birth. Mahamati, what is the imagining of non-birth? It is this: all natures are originally unborn; without the causes and conditions of a seed, a body without a cause is born. This is called the imagining of non-birth. Mahamati, what is the imagining of continuity? It is this: those continuing together, like a thread of gold. This is called the imagining of continuity. Mahamati, what is the imagining of bondage and non-bondage? It is this: the grasping at the causes and conditions of bondage — as a man by expedients is either bound or released. This is called the imagining of bondage and non-bondage. As to these marks of the distinctions of the self-nature of imagining, all foolish ordinary beings grasp at being and non-being. Mahamati, those who grasp at dependent origination grasp at the self-nature of various imaginings. As an illusion manifests various bodies, so foolish ordinary beings imagine, and see various illusions as different. Mahamati, the illusion and the various things are neither different nor not different. If they were different, the illusion would not be the cause of the various things; if they were not different, the illusion and the various things would have no distinction, yet a distinction is seen. Therefore they are neither different nor not different. Therefore, Mahamati, you and the other great bodhisattvas should not grasp at difference or non-difference, being or non-being, as to the self-nature of the imagining of illusion-like dependent origination.”
Bound to the field of objects, thought and awareness turn along with it,
from the nothing and the supreme alike, the wisdom of evenness is born.
Discrimination’s own-nature has being; in dependent arising it is naught,
discrimination may grasp and receive, yet dependent arising is no discrimination.
The manifold branches are produced, but as illusion they do not stand,
those marks are manifold, and yet discrimination does not stand.
Those marks are the very fault, born all from the bondage of the mind,
discrimination knows nothing, yet discriminates dependent arising.
This very nature of discrimination is that dependent arising,
discrimination is of many kinds, yet it discriminates dependent arising.
Worldly truth and ultimate truth, and a third that is born without a cause,
discrimination speaks of worldly truth; when cut off, there is the sage’s realm.
As in the work of practice, within the One the many appear,
yet within it there is no plurality; such is the mark of discrimination.
As with the many film-veils, discrimination shows the many colors,
the film has color and no color; in arising it is not thus discerned.
As when refining genuine gold, far removed from every stain,
the sky is free of cloud and film; so has discrimination been made pure.
There is no nature of discrimination, and no such dependent arising,
assertion and repudiation alike are wholly ruined by discrimination.
If discrimination has no nature, yet there is a nature of arising,
then from no nature a nature comes, and existence is born of nonexistence.
Relying on discrimination, one obtains that dependent arising,
name and mark forever accompany, and give rise to discriminations.
When in the end it is not accomplished, one then crosses discrimination,
and thereafter knows the purity; this is called the ultimate truth.
Discrimination has twelve kinds; dependent arising has six,
self-awakened knowledge; between these there is no difference.
The five dharmas are the real; own-nature has three kinds,
the practitioner discriminates these, yet never oversteps the Suchness.
The marks and dependent arising; their names give rise to discrimination,
and those marks of discrimination are born from that dependent arising.
Awakened insight well observes: no conditions, no discrimination,
when accomplished there is no nature; how then does discrimination wake?
That discrimination own-nature establishes the two own-natures,
discrimination appears in many forms; purity is the sage’s realm.
Discrimination is as the colors in a painting; arising contrives discrimination,
if it were other than discrimination, it would follow the heterodox teachings.
Discrimination speaks of what is thought, born of the union of the views,
free of the two discriminations, thus is it accomplished.”

Mahamati the great bodhisattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, please teach the marks of the self-awakened sage-knowledge and of the One Vehicle. If you teach the marks of the self-awakened sage-knowledge and the One Vehicle, then I and the other bodhisattvas, being well awakened to the marks of the self-awakened sage-knowledge and the One Vehicle, shall understand the Buddha-Dharma without depending on another.”
The Buddha told Mahamati: “Listen well, listen well; think upon it well. I shall speak it for you.”
Mahamati said to the Buddha: “So be it; I receive your instruction.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “The object known by the former sages, handed down from one to another, is that discrimination has no nature. The great bodhisattva, alone in a quiet place, contemplates with self-awakening, not depending on another, free from the discriminations of views, advancing ever upward, enters the ground of the Tathagata; this is called the mark of the self-awakened sage-knowledge. Mahamati, what is the mark of the One Vehicle? It is this: having attained the awareness of the One Vehicle path, I speak of the One Vehicle. How is the awareness of the One Vehicle path attained? It is this: what is grasped and the grasping, in the abode of reality, gives rise to no discrimination; this is called the awareness of the One Vehicle. Mahamati, the awareness of the One Vehicle is not to be attained by the heterodox, the shravakas, the pratyekabuddhas, the Brahma kings and the like, but only by the Tathagata. Because of this it is called the One Vehicle.”
Mahamati said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, why does the World-Honored One speak of three vehicles, and not of the One Vehicle?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “Because it is not the Dharma of self-parinirvana, I do not say that all shravakas and pratyekabuddhas are the One Vehicle. Since all shravakas and pratyekabuddhas are tamed by the Tathagata, given the expedient of tranquility, and so attain liberation, not by their own power, therefore I do not speak of the One Vehicle.

Moreover, Mahamati! Because the habit-energy of the karmic affliction-obstruction is not cut off, I do not say that all shravakas and pratyekabuddhas are the One Vehicle. Not realizing the non-self of dharmas, not leaving the death of the delimited, therefore I speak of three vehicles. Mahamati, those whose habit-energies of all the arising afflictions are cut off, and who realize the non-self of dharmas — when the habit-energies of all the arising afflictions are cut off, they do not taste the flavor of the bliss of samadhi as an entity, and realize the taint-free realm. Having realized it, they again enter the supreme taint-free realm beyond the world, fulfilling all the requisites, and shall attain the inconceivable self-mastery of the Tathagata’s Dharma-body.”
The vehicle of the devas and of Brahma, the vehicle of shravaka and pratyekabuddha,
the vehicle of the Buddhas and the Tathagatas; I speak of all these vehicles,
yet so long as the mind turns, all the vehicles are not ultimate.
If that mind is extinguished, there is no vehicle and no rider,
no vehicle is established; I call it the One Vehicle,
and to guide sentient beings, I distinguish and speak the several vehicles.
Liberation is of three kinds, along with the non-self of dharmas,
afflictions, wisdom and the like; liberation is far from them all.
As a plank of driftwood on the sea, forever turning with the waves,
so too the foolish shravakas, blown about by the wind of marks.
Their arising afflictions cease; the habitual folly of the defilements remains,
they taste the bliss of samadhi, and abide in the taint-free realm.
They have no final goal, and yet they do not fall back,
attaining the bodies of the samadhis, and for an eon still not awake.
As one who is drunk, when the wine subsides, then wakes,
so too when they awaken to dharmas, they attain the Buddha’s supreme body.”
The Lankavatara Sutra, Fascicle Three
The Heart of the Buddha’s Words, Part Three

At that time the World-Honored One said to Mahamati the great bodhisattva: “The general marks of the mind-made body and its discrimination, I shall now speak. Listen well, listen well; think upon it well.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “There are three mind-made bodies. What are the three? They are: the mind-made body of the samadhi of bliss and right absorption; the mind-made body that realizes the own-nature of dharmas; and the mind-made body born together with all kinds, without acting. The practitioner, knowing the marks of successive advancement upon the grounds, attains these three bodies. Mahamati, what is the mind-made body of the samadhi of bliss and right absorption? It is this: because of the bliss of samadhi and right absorption on the third, fourth and fifth grounds, the various self-minds are stilled, abiding in the ocean of mind, where the marks of the rising waves of consciousness do not arise; knowing that the objects manifesting from one’s own mind have a nature and no-nature; this is called the mind-made body of the samadhi of bliss and right absorption. Mahamati, what is the mind-made body that realizes the own-nature of dharmas? It is this: upon the eighth ground, observing and realizing that dharmas, like illusion, are all without anything whatever, the body and mind are transformed, attaining the samadhi of illusion and the other samadhi-gates, with boundless marks, empowered by self-mastery and light, adorned like exquisite flowers, swift as the will, like illusion, dream, the moon in water and a mirror-image, neither made nor maker, like made and yet unmade, with all forms and their manifold members fully adorned, entering the great assemblies of all the Buddha-fields, because it penetrates the own-nature of dharmas; this is called the mind-made body that realizes the own-nature of dharmas. Mahamati, what is the mind-made body born together with all kinds, without acting? It is this: realizing all the Buddha-dharmas, and the mark of the bliss self-obtained; this is called the mind-made body born together with all kinds, without acting. Mahamati, observing and realizing these three marks of body, one should cultivate and learn them.”
Not my vehicle, not the Great Vehicle, not spoken, nor a word,
not a truth, not liberation, and not the realm of nothing.
But the Mahayana, self-mastery of samadhi,
the various mind-made bodies, freely adorned with flowers.”

At that time Mahamati the great bodhisattva said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has declared, if a man or a woman commits the five inexpiable acts, he does not fall into the Avici hell. World-Honored One, how is it that a man or a woman who commits the five inexpiable acts does not fall into the Avici hell?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “What are the five inexpiable acts? They are: the killing of father and mother, the injuring of the arhat, the disrupting of the assembly of monks, and, with an evil mind, the causing of the Buddha’s body to bleed. Mahamati, what is the mother of beings? It is the craving of thirst that renews birth, accompanied by greed and joy; as a mother stands upon the cause of birth. Ignorance is the father. From these one is born into the village of the six sense-fields; cutting off these two roots is called injuring father and mother. When those defilements do not appear, like the poison of a rat breaking out, and are cut off in the ultimate, this is called injuring the arhat. What is disrupting the sangha? The aggregates of differing marks gathered and accumulated, cut off in the ultimate; this is called disrupting the sangha. Mahamati, not realizing the self-common marks of external objects, and the body of the seven consciousnesses as the measure of one’s own mind, with the taint-free evil-thought of the three liberations, cutting off in the ultimate that sevenfold consciousness-Buddha; this is called, with an evil mind, causing the Buddha’s body to bleed. If a man or a woman commits these inexpiable deeds, they are called the five inexpiable matters, and are also called the five inexpiable acts.

Moreover, Mahamati, there are the outward inexpiable acts; I shall now expound them. When you and the other great bodhisattvas have heard this meaning, in ages to come you will not fall into ignorance. What are the five inexpiable acts? They are those inexpiable acts spoken of before. If one commits them, among the three liberations he does not at all attain the equal Dharmas of no-interruption. Apart from this Dharma, the rest are the transformation-powers that manifest the equal no-interruption: namely, the transformation-power of the shravakas, the transformation-power of the bodhisattvas, and the transformation-power of the Tathagatas, which, for the sake of those who commit the inexpiable acts, to remove their doubt and remorse and to exhort them, work by power and transformation, manifesting the equal no-interruption. No one who has committed the inexpiable deed throughout attains the equal Dharma of no-interruption, apart from realizing the measure of the self-manifestations of their own mind, free from the discriminations of body and possessions, free from the grasping of self and mine. Sometimes, meeting a good teacher, one is liberated from the continuous discriminations of other realms.”
Craving and love are called the mother; ignorance is the father,
the consciousness of the perceived realm is the Buddha; the defilements are the arhat,
the gathering of the aggregates is the sangha; in unbroken sequence cut off,
these are called the five inexpiable acts, which do not enter the Avici prison.”

At that time Mahamati the great bodhisattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, please teach the Buddha’s knowledge and perception. World-Honored One, what is the Buddha’s knowledge and perception?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “Realizing the non-self of persons and of dharmas, knowing the two obstructions, free from the two deaths, cutting off the two afflictions; this is called the Buddha’s knowledge and perception. Shravakas and pratyekabuddhas who attain this Dharma are also called Buddhas. Because of this reason, I speak of the One Vehicle.”
Well knowing the two non-selves, the two obstructions and afflictions cut off,
forever free of the two deaths; this is called the Buddha’s knowledge.”

At that time Mahamati said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, why does the World-Honored One, in the midst of the great assembly, proclaim such words as these: ‘I am all the past Buddhas, and of many and various births; at that time I was the wheel-turning sage-king Mandhata, the six-tusked elephant, the parrot, Shakra, the seer of the good eye, and so forth, through hundreds of thousands of births, as the sutras relate?’” The Buddha told Mahamati: “Because of the four equalities, the Tathagata, Arhat, and perfect Buddha, in the midst of the great assembly, proclaim such words: ‘At that time I was Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kashyapa Buddha.’ What are the four equalities? The equality of words, the equality of speech, the equality of Dharma, and the equality of body; these are called the four equalities. Because of these four equalities, the Tathagata, Arhat, and perfect Buddha, in the midst of the great assembly, proclaim such words. What is the equality of words? If by a word I am called a Buddha, that same word is also given to all the Buddhas; the own-nature of that word has no difference; this is called the equality of words. What is the equality of speech? It is this: my sixty-four kinds of Brahman-voice and speech-marks arise; those Tathagatas, Arhats, and perfect Buddhas likewise have such sixty-four kinds of Brahman-voice and speech-marks, without increase or decrease, without difference, the voice-nature of the kalavinka. What is the equality of body? It is this: my Dharma-body and form-body, with their marks and excellence, have no difference from those of the Buddhas, except that to tame the beings of the various different destinies, they display various different form-bodies; this is called the equality of body. What is the equality of Dharma? It is this: I and those Buddhas obtain the thirty-seven factors of bodhi; in brief, the Buddha-Dharma is the unobstructed wisdom; this is called the four equalities. Therefore the Tathagata, Arhat, and perfect Buddha, in the midst of the great assembly, proclaim such words.”
Kashyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni are I,
because of these four equalities, I declare it to the Buddha’s children.”

Mahamati again said to the Buddha: “As the World-Honored One has declared: ‘I attained the most perfect enlightenment on a certain night, and on a certain night entered parinirvana; in between, not a single word was spoken, nor has been spoken, nor will be spoken; that which is not spoken, this is said to be spoken by the Buddha.’”
Mahamati said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, for what reason does the Tathagata, Arhat, and perfect Buddha say: ‘that which is not spoken is spoken by the Buddha’?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “Because of two dharmas I speak thus. What are the two? They are the Dharma self-obtained, and the abiding Dharma; these are called the two dharmas. Because of these two dharmas I speak thus. What is the Dharma self-obtained? What the Tathagata has obtained, I have also obtained, without increase or decrease. The ultimate realm of the self-obtained Dharma, free from the discriminations of words, free from the two courses of words. What is the abiding Dharma? It is the ancient path of the former sages. Like the nature of gold and silver, the Dharma-realm abides forever; whether the Tathagata appears in the world or not, the Dharma-realm abides forever. As one approaches that attained way, for instance, a man walking in the wilderness sees the even, true road to an ancient city, and straightway enters the city, enjoying the bliss of its delights. Mahamati, what do you think? Did that man make that road and the various delights of the city?”
He answered: “No.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “The Dharma-realm of me and of all the past Buddhas abides forever, just so. Therefore it is said: ‘I attained the most perfect enlightenment on a certain night, and on a certain night entered parinirvana; in between, not a single word was spoken, nor has been, nor will be.’”
On a certain night I attained the way; on a certain night I entered nirvana,
between these two, I had nothing at all to say.
Because of the self-obtained and abiding Dharma, I speak thus,
that Buddha and I are wholly without difference.”

At that time Mahamati the great bodhisattva again requested the World-Honored One: “Please teach the marks of the existence and non-existence of all dharmas, so that I and the other great bodhisattvas, freed from the marks of existence and non-existence, may quickly attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “The world relies on two kinds: namely, on existence and on non-existence; and falls into the desire to see the nature and non-nature, without leaving the marks of separation. Mahamati, what is the world’s reliance on existence? It is that existence is born of the causes and conditions of the world, not non-existence; born from existence, not from non-existence. Mahamati, one who speaks thus is saying that the world has no cause. Mahamati, what is the world’s reliance on non-existence? Having grasped the nature of greed, hatred and delusion, one then discriminates and grasps the nature of greed, hatred and delusion as non-nature. Mahamati, if one does not grasp the nature of existence, the marks of nature are still. Therefore the Tathagatas, the shravakas and the pratyekabuddhas do not grasp the nature of greed, hatred and delusion as existent or non-existent. Mahamati, what here is the ruiner?”
Mahamati said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, it is when one grasps the nature of greed, hatred and delusion, and thereafter does not again grasp it.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “Well said, well said. You understand thus. Mahamati, it is not only the non-nature of greed, hatred and delusion that is the ruiner; for the shravakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddha too, it is also a ruiner. Why is it so? Because inner and outer are unattainable, and because the nature of the afflictions is both different and not different. Mahamati, greed, hatred and delusion are unattainable whether inner or outer; because the nature of greed, hatred and delusion has no body and no grasping, the Buddha, the shravakas and the pratyekabuddhas are not the ruiners. Because the Buddha, the shravakas and the pratyekabuddhas are self-liberated by nature, since bondage and the cause of bondage are of no nature. Mahamati, if there is a bound one, there must be bondage as its cause. Mahamati, one who speaks thus is a ruiner; this is called the mark of the all-less. Mahamati, because of this, I say that one had better grasp the view of self as great as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to the prideful empty view of the all-less. Mahamati, those prideful in the all-less are called ruiners. Falling into the hope of self-common marks, not knowing the measure of the self-manifestations of one’s own mind; seeing outer natures as impermanent, destroyed in an instant and turning onward; the aggregates, realms and bases continuously flowing and changing, gone forever from the discriminations of the marks of words; this is called the ruiner.”
Existence and non-existence are the two extremes; even to the sphere of the mind,
purify that sphere, and the mind of evenness is stilled.
Not grasping the nature of the realm, extinction is not an all-less,
whatever is, is the Suchness, even as the sages’ realm.
Without a seed yet born, born and then again destroyed,
causes and conditions are existent and non-existent; they abide not in my teaching.
Not of the heterodox, not of the Buddha; not self, and not another,
gathered by causes and conditions, how can it be nothing at all?
Who gathers causes and conditions into existence, and then speaks of non-existence?
The heterodox discourse of the birth of dharmas, discriminating existence and non-existence.
If one knows that nothing is born, and likewise nothing is destroyed,
observing all this as utterly empty and still, both existence and non-existence are left behind.”

At that time Mahamati the great bodhisattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, please teach, for me and the bodhisattvas, the marks of the matter-awakening and the principle-understanding. If we are well able to discriminate the marks of the matter-awakening and the principle-understanding, then I and the bodhisattvas shall penetrate these marks, and having penetrated them, quickly accomplish anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, without following the discriminations of perception and the host of demons and the heterodox.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “All shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas have two kinds of penetration-marks, namely the matter-awakening and the word-awakening. Mahamati, the matter-awakening is this: relying on the mark of the self-obtained supreme advancement, far from the discriminations of words and letters, going to the taint-free realm, the self-mark of self-awakening, far from all false perceptions and discriminative thought, subduing all the heterodox and the hosts of demons, relying on the realm of self-awakening, luminous and blooming. This is called the mark of the matter-awakening. What is the mark of the word-awakening? It is the teaching of the nine-limbed and various discourses, free from the marks of different and not different, of existence and non-existence, and with skillful means, in accord with sentient beings, teaching the Dharma as is fitting, so that they attain deliverance. This is called the mark of the word-awakening. Mahamati, you and the other bodhisattvas should cultivate and learn it.”
