At that time the bodhisattva Mahāmati said to the Buddha: ‘O Blessed One, may the Blessed One be pleased to speak of the truly and fully enlightened Buddha. Then I and the other bodhisattvas-mahāsattvas will be skilled in the Tathāgata’s self-nature, awakening self and awakening others.’
The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘Ask as you wish, and I will speak to you in accordance with your question.’

Mahāmati said to the Buddha: ‘O Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Worthy of Offerings, the Fully Enlightened One — is he the maker? Or the not-maker? Is he the action? Or the cause? Is he the characteristic? Or the characterized? Is he the speaker? Or the spoken? Is he the awakener? Or the awakened? Are such phrases as these different or not different?’

The Buddha told Mahamati, 'The Tathagata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, with regard to these various phrases, is neither a thing nor a cause. Why? Because both involve faults. Mahamati! If the Tathagata were a thing, he would be either created or impermanent. Being impermanent, all things should be the Tathagata. Neither I nor all the Buddhas would wish this. If he is not created, then because nothing is attained, the expedient means would be empty, like a hare's horn or the son of a barren woman, because of having no existence at all. Mahamati! If there is neither thing nor cause, then it is neither existing nor non-existing. If neither existing nor non-existing, then it transcends the four propositions. The four propositions pertain to worldly speech. If one transcends the four propositions, one does not fall into them. Not falling into them, this is taken up by the wise. The meaning of all the Tathagatas' phrases is likewise thus; the wise should know it. As I have said, all dharmas are without self. Know this meaning: the nature of non-self is non-self. All dharmas have their own self-nature, and no other nature, like a cow or a horse. Mahamati! For example, that which is neither cow-nature nor horse-nature is the horse-nature and the cow-nature. In truth it is neither existing nor non-existing; they are not without their own marks. Thus, Mahamati! All dharmas are not without self-mark, yet have self-mark; but this is not something that foolish people can know. Because of delusion, all dharmas are thus empty, unborn, without self-nature. Thus should it be known. Likewise, the Tathagata and the aggregates are neither different nor not different. If not different from the aggregates, he should be impermanent. If different, then the expedient means would be empty. If they are both, there should be a difference. Like the horns of an ox: being similar, they are not different; being different in length and shortness, they are different. All dharmas are likewise. Mahamati! As the right horn of an ox differs from the left horn, and the left horn from the right, so in length and shortness and the various colors each one differs. Mahamati! The Tathagata, with regard to the aggregates, realms, and sense-fields, is neither different nor not different. Likewise, the Tathagata's liberation is neither different nor not different. Thus the Tathagata is spoken of as the name of liberation. If the Tathagata were different from liberation, he should be accomplished by form-marks; being accomplished by form-marks, he should be impermanent. If not different, then the cultivator would attain the corresponding non-discrimination, yet the cultivator sees discrimination. Therefore he is neither different nor not different. Likewise, knowledge and its object are neither different nor not different. Mahamati! Knowledge and its object, being neither different nor not different, are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither created nor uncreated, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither that which knows nor that which is known, neither mark nor what is marked, neither the aggregates nor other than the aggregates, neither spoken nor what is spoken, neither one nor many, neither both nor neither. Because they are neither one nor many, neither both nor neither, they are wholly free from all measure
what is seen, heard, cognized, and known is called measure

. Free from all measure, there is no speech. No speech, then no arising. No arising, then no ceasing. No ceasing, then quiescence. Quiescence, then self-nature nirvana. Self-nature nirvana, then neither thing nor cause. Neither thing nor cause, then no clinging. No clinging, then transcending all falsehood. Transcending all falsehood, then this is the Tathagata. The Tathagata is then samyak-sambuddha. Mahamati! This is called samyak-sambuddha. The Buddha is free from all the measures of the faculties.'
Freed from every measure of the faculties,
neither thing nor cause is found;
Already freed from the known and the knower, freed also from mark and what is marked.
Skandhas and cause and the Perfectly Enlightened One, one and many cannot be seen;
If there is no one who sees, how can there be discrimination?
Neither made nor not made, neither thing nor cause;
Neither in the skandhas nor apart from them, nor yet in any other mingling;
Nor yet possessed of any nature, as deluded views imagine.
Know also that it is not non-existent; this Dharma is thus of itself;
Because of existence there is non-existence, because of non-existence there is existence;
What is non-existent should not be accepted, what is existent should not be conceived.
Or with regard to self and non-self, lingering over the measures of speech,
Sinking in the two extremes, they ruin themselves and ruin the world.
Freed from all faults, rightly observing my penetration,
This is called right contemplation, and does not defame the great Guide.'

Then the Bodhisattva Mahamati again said to the Buddha, 'World-Honored One! As the World-Honored One has said, the sutras take up the unborn and the unceasing. And the World-Honored One also says that the unborn and the unceasing is another name for the Tathagata. How is it, World-Honored One, that you speak of the unborn and the unceasing for the sake of non-nature? Or is it another name for the Tathagata?'
The Buddha told Mahamati, 'I say that all dharmas are unborn and unceasing, and that the categories of existence and non-existence do not appear.'

Mahamati said to the Buddha, 'World-Honored One! If all dharmas are unborn, then the dharmas that are taken up are unattainable, since all dharmas are unborn. If there is any dharma in names, I beg you to explain it.'
The Buddha told Mahamati, 'Well said! Well said! Listen attentively and think upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.'

The Buddha told Mahamati, 'I say that the Tathagata is not non-nature, nor is he the unborn and unceasing that takes in all dharmas, nor is he unborn and unceasing by depending on conditions, nor is he without meaning. Mahamati! I speak of the Tathagata as the name of the mind-born dharmakaya. That which is unborn is not the province of all the externalists, the sravakas, the pratyekabuddhas, or the bodhisattvas of the seventh abode. Mahamati! That unborn is another name for the Tathagata. Mahamati! For example, Indra, Shakra, Pulandara — such things each have many names; nor is it because of many names that there is many a nature, nor is it without self-nature. Thus, Mahamati! In this Saha world
Saha means able to endure

, I have three hundred thousand million names; foolish people have all heard of them, and each speaks of my name, yet they do not understand that they are other names of the Tathagata. Mahamati! There are beings who know me as the Tathagata, who know me as the all-knowing one, as the Buddha, as the savior of the world, as the self-awakened, as the guide, as the wide guide, as the guide of all, as the sage, as Brahma, as Vishnu, as the sovereign, as the supreme, as Kapila, as the truth-boundary, as the moon, as the sun, as the unborn, as the unceasing, as the empty, as thusness, as truth, as actual reality, as dharmatā, as nirvana, as the permanent, as the equal, as the non-dual, as the markless, as liberation, as the Way, as the mind-born. Mahamati! These three hundred thousand million names neither increase nor decrease. In this and in other worlds all know me, as the moon reflected in water, neither going out nor coming in. Those foolish people cannot know me because they fall into the two extremes. Yet they all respectfully make offerings to me, but do not well understand the meaning and drift of the phrases, do not discriminate the names, do not understand self-mastery, and cling to various letters and sentences. With regard to the unborn and unceasing they entertain the notion of non-nature. They do not know that the names of the Tathagata are different, like Indra, Shakra, Pulandara. They do not understand self-mastery, nor go back to what is ultimate. With regard to all dharmas they cling to whatever is spoken. Mahamati! Those foolish people say thus: 'Meaning is like speech; meaning and speech are no different. Why? Because meaning has no body; apart from speech there is no other meaning, and there is only speech.' Mahamati! Their wisdom is burned by evil; they do not know the self-nature of speech, nor that speech is born and ceases, while meaning neither arises nor ceases. Mahamati! All speech falls into letters; meaning does not fall. Being apart from nature and non-nature, it has no arising, and also no body. Mahamati! The Tathagata does not speak of dharmas that fall into letters, because existence and non-existence of letters are unattainable, except for what does not fall into letters. Mahamati! If anyone says that the Tathagata speaks of dharmas that fall into letters, this is a false assertion, because the Dharma is apart from letters. Therefore, Mahamati! We Buddhas and bodhisattvas speak not a single word and answer not a single word. Why? Because the Dharma is apart from letters. Not that we do not speak what benefits the meaning. Speech arises from the delusion of sentient beings. Mahamati! If one does not speak all dharmas, the teaching is destroyed. If the teaching is destroyed, then there are no Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, or sravakas. If there are none, who speaks, and to whom? Therefore, Mahamati! The bodhisattva-mahasattva should not cling to speech, but according to what is expedient should broadly proclaim the scriptures. Because the hopes and afflictions of sentient beings are not one, I and the Buddhas speak the various dharmas for those beings with different understandings, in order to free them from mind, thought, and consciousness, and not for the attainment of the state of self-realized noble wisdom. Mahamati! In all dharmas there is nothing whatsoever; realizing the self-nature of mind's appearances, one is free from the two discriminations. The bodhisattva-mahasattva relies on meaning, not on letters. If good men and good women rely on letters, they ruin the first principle themselves and cannot awaken others. Falling into evil views, they speak for the assembly, and not well understanding all dharmas, all grounds, and all marks, they do not know the phrases. If one understands all dharmas, all grounds, and all marks, and penetrates the phrases, being endowed with the nature of meaning, then he can rejoice in the right markless joy and establish sentient beings in the great vehicle of equality. Mahamati! One who takes up the great vehicle takes up all the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and sravakas. One who takes up all the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and sravakas takes up all sentient beings. One who takes up all sentient beings takes up the right Dharma. One who takes up the right Dharma keeps the Buddha-seed uninterrupted. One who keeps the Buddha-seed uninterrupted can know and attain the supreme abode. Knowing and attaining the supreme abode, the bodhisattva-mahasattva is always born miraculously and establishes the great vehicle. With the ten powers of self-mastery, he manifests all forms. He penetrates the forms, hopes, and afflictions of beings, and speaks the Dharma truly. True reality is not different. True reality is free from the marks of coming and going; all falsehood is stilled. This is called true reality. Mahamati! Good men and good women should not take up what is spoken and cling to it; for the true is apart from letters. Mahamati! As when one points at an object with a finger for the sake of a foolish person, the fool looks at the finger and does not get the real meaning. Thus foolish people, following the finger of speech, cling to it and never let it go, and in the end cannot attain the first true meaning which is apart from the finger of speech. Mahamati! As an infant should eat cooked food and not raw; if it eats raw, it becomes crazed, because it does not know the order and the skill of cooking. Thus, Mahamati! The unborn and the unceasing, if not cultivated by the expedient means, becomes not good. Therefore one should well cultivate the expedient means and not follow speech, like gazing at the tip of a finger. Therefore, Mahamati! With regard to true meaning, one should cultivate the expedient means. True meaning is subtle and still, and is the cause of nirvana. Speech is conjoined with delusion. Delusion accumulates birth-and-death. Mahamati! True meaning is obtained from one who has heard much. Mahamati! One who has heard much is one who is good in meaning, not one who is good in speech. One who is good in meaning does not follow the treatises of the externalists; he himself does not follow them, nor does he cause others to follow them. This is called a great and virtuous one who has heard much. Therefore one who seeks meaning should draw near to one who has heard much — that is, one who is good in meaning should draw near to one who has heard much, that is, one who is good in meaning. Contrariwise, one who clings to speech should be avoided.'

Then the Bodhisattva Mahamati, again relying on the Buddha's spiritual power, said to the Buddha, 'World-Honored One! The World-Honored One demonstrates the unborn and the unceasing, but there is nothing wonderful in it. Why? All the externalists also speak of the unborn and the unceasing as cause. The World-Honored One also speaks of space, of non-analytical cessation, and of the realm of nirvana as unborn and unceasing. World-Honored One! The externalists say that a cause gives rise to the worlds. The World-Honored One also says that ignorance, craving, karma, and delusion as conditions give rise to the worlds. These causes and conditions differ only in name; the external conditions also are thus. Thus, World-Honored One, there is no difference from the doctrines of the externalists. Atoms, the supreme, the sovereign, the lord of beings — such nine things are unborn and unceasing. The World-Honored One also says that all natures are unborn and unceasing, and that existence and non-existence are unattainable. The externalists also say that the four great elements are indestructible and that their self-nature is unborn and unceasing. The four great elements are permanent. These four great elements, even as they flow through the various destinies, do not give up their self-nature. What the World-Honored One says is also thus. Therefore I say there is nothing wonderful in it. I beg the World-Honored One to tell the difference, and wherein it is wonderful and surpasses the externalists. If there is no difference, then all externalists are also Buddhas, because of the unborn and the unceasing. Yet the World-Honored One says that there is no such thing as many Buddhas appearing in one world. As said earlier, in one world there should be many Buddhas, because there is no difference.'

The Buddha told Mahamati, 'My unborn and unceasing is different from the unborn and unceasing of the externalists. Why? Those externalists have a self-nature of being, and attain a nature that is unborn and unchanging. I am not thus, falling into the categories of existence and non-existence. Mahamati! I am free from the categories of existence and non-existence, free from arising and ceasing, neither nature nor non-nature. Because various illusions and dreams appear, it is not non-nature. How is it non-nature? Because form has no self-nature mark that is taken up, appearing and not appearing, taken and not taken. For this reason, all natures are non-nature and yet not non-nature; but by realizing the self-nature of mind's appearances, discrimination does not arise, and there is peaceful happiness, and worldly affairs cease forever. Foolish ordinary people create things by discrimination; this is not the noble sages' way. Unreal discrimination is like a gandharva city, and like magically conjured beings. Mahamati! As in a gandharva city and among magically conjured beings, various beings and merchants go in and out. Foolish people imagine a true going in and out, but in truth there is no one who goes out or comes in; it is only their discrimination. Thus, Mahamati! Foolish ordinary people give rise to the notion of the unborn and the unceasing, yet there is also no conditioned or unconditioned. As a conjured being is born, in truth there is no birth or death, because nature and non-nature are all non-existent. All dharmas are also thus, apart from arising and ceasing. Foolish ordinary people, falling into the non-true, give rise to the discrimination of arising and ceasing; this is not the noble sages' way. What is non-true is not thus. The discrimination of nature and self-nature is also not different. If it were different from discrimination, one would cling to the self-nature of all natures and not see stillness. Not seeing stillness, one never departs from discrimination. Therefore, Mahamati! The markless is superior. What has the marks of marks is the cause of rebirth, and so is not superior. Mahamati! The markless: where discrimination does not arise, neither arising nor ceasing, I call this nirvana. Mahamati! Nirvana is seen as true meaning, free from the former discriminations and the dharmas of mind and mental factors, and attaining the Tathagata's self-realized noble wisdom; this I call nirvana.'
Destroying the theories of becoming,
I establish the meaning of the unborn;
I speak such a Dharma, which the foolish cannot know.
All dharmas are unborn, without nature, without anything;
Like a gandharva city, an illusion, a dream; what has nature has no cause,
Unborn and without self-nature; for what cause should emptiness be spoken?
Because of being apart from combination, the nature of knowing does not appear;
Therefore emptiness is unborn; I speak of the absence of self-nature.
As for each combination, the nature appears and yet is not;
When analyzed there is no combination, which is not as the externalists see.
Like a dream, like a mirage of the hair, a mirage, a gandharva city,
The many things of the world appear as marks, yet without a cause.
I refute the theory of causation and set forth the meaning of the unborn.
One who sets forth the unborn keeps the stream of Dharma forever unbroken,
And with the blazing theory of no-cause strikes terror into the externalists.
Why and for what cause, from what does it arise,
In what place does it combine, that one makes the theory of no-cause?
Observing the conditioned dharmas, neither without cause nor with cause,
The advocates of arising and ceasing have their views extinguished by this.
What is meant by the unborn? Is it the absence of nature?
Or, looking to the various conditions, is there a dharma named the unborn?
A name should not be without meaning; only for the sake of discrimination I speak,
It is not the unborn of non-nature, nor looking to the various conditions;
Nor is there a nature and a name; the name is not without meaning.
All the externalists, the sravakas, and the pratyekabuddhas,
The seventh abode is not their province; this is called the mark of the unborn.
Far from the various conditions and far from all things,
With only the subtle mind dwelling, thought and what is thought both left behind,
Its body following the transformation, I call this the unborn.
With no outer nature and no non-nature, and also no grasping of the mind,
Cutting off all views, I call this the unborn.
Thus the absence of self-nature, emptiness, and so forth should be discriminated:
It is not emptiness because of emptiness, but emptiness because of the unborn.
When the conditions and the elements combine, then there is arising and ceasing;
Apart from the enumeration of conditions, there is no separate arising or ceasing.
Abandoning the enumeration of conditions, there is still no other nature;
To speak of one or of difference is the delusion of the externalists.
The unborn of existence and non-existence; neither existent nor non-existent,
Apart from the permutations of the enumeration, all this is unattainable.
There are only the conventions of the world, turning onward like a chain of hooks,
Apart from that chain of causes and conditions, the meaning of arising is unattainable.
What is born, being without nature, does not rise — this leaves behind the faults of the externalists;
But I speak only of the chain of conditions, which the foolish cannot understand.
If apart from the chain of conditions there were another nature of birth,
that would be the theory of no-cause, and would destroy the meaning of the chain.
As a lamp reveals all forms, the chain appears in this way;
then, apart from the chain, there would yet be other natures.
The natureless that is unborn, like the self-nature of empty space,
if apart from the chain, then wisdom has nothing to discriminate.
There is yet another unborn, the Dharma attained by the noble sages;
that birth which is unborn
that birth is the birth of the four marks
this is the patient endurance of the unborn. If the worlds,
observing the chain, all are apart from the chain,
then from this they obtain samadhi. Delusion, craving, karma, and so forth,
these are the inner chain; the fire-stick, the clay ball, the wheel,
and the seed are called the outer. If there were another nature
arising from causes and conditions, that would not be the meaning of the chain,
and would not be accomplished. If birth is without self-nature,
for whom is there a chain? Because they arise in mutual dependence,
know the meaning of causes and conditions. If birth had another nature,
it would not be accomplished. The dharmas of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion,
foolish people give rise to delusion about; apart from the enumeration there is no other dharma,
and this is called naturelessness. As a physician cures all diseases,
there are not many theories; because of the differences in illness,
he sets up various treatments. For those beings,
I destroy the various afflictions, knowing the superior and inferior of their faculties,
and for them speak the gates of deliverance. It is not that the roots of affliction differ
and so there are various dharmas; I speak only the single vehicle Dharma,
and this is the great vehicle.'

Then the Bodhisattva Mahamati again said to the Buddha, 'World-Honored One! All the externalists give rise to the delusion of impermanence. The World-Honored One also speaks of all formations as impermanent, as the dharmas of arising and ceasing. What is the meaning of this? Is it wrong or right? How many kinds of impermanence are there?'

The Buddha told Mahamati, 'All the externalists have seven kinds of impermanence; they are not my Dharma. What are the seven? There are some who say: having been made and then abandoned, this is called impermanence. Some say the destruction of shape and place is impermanence. Some say that form itself is impermanence. Some say that in the midst of the transformation of form there is impermanence. There is also the impermanence of the nature of natures, the impermanence of nature and non-nature, and the impermanence of the non-arising of all dharmas, entering into all dharmas. Mahamati! The impermanence of nature and non-nature means the destruction of the self-marks of the four great elements and what they produce. The self-nature of the four great elements is unattainable and is unborn. That unborn impermanence is neither permanent nor impermanent. All dharmas, whether existent or non-existent, do not arise; when analyzed down to atoms they are not seen — this is the meaning of the unborn, not of birth; this is called the mark of the unborn impermanence. If one does not awaken to this, one falls into the meaning of the birth-impermanence of all the externalists. Mahamati! As for the impermanence of natures, it is the self-mind's discrimination, not the nature of the permanent or the impermanent. Why? Because the self-nature of impermanence is not destroyed. Mahamati! This is the matter of the impermanence of the naturelessness of all natures. Apart from impermanence, there is nothing that can cause the naturelessness of all dharmas. As a staff, a tile, or a stone break up various things, so in direct perception each and every one is not different — this is the matter of the impermanence of natures, and there is no difference between agent and deed. This is impermanence; this is matter. Where the agent and the deed are not different, all natures are permanent and have no cause-nature. Mahamati! That all natures are natureless has a cause, which is not known by the foolish; nor is it that a non-similar cause gives rise to things. If it did, all natures would all be impermanent. This is the non-similar thing. The agent and the deed have no distinction, yet all are seen to be different. If natures were impermanent, they would fall into the nature-marks of the agent-cause. If they fall into these, then all natures are not final. If all natures fall into the nature-marks of a cause, self-impermanence should be impermanent. Since impermanence is impermanent, all natures are not impermanent and should be permanent. If impermanence enters all natures, it should fall into the three times. Past form is together with destruction; the future is not born; because form is unborn, present form is together with the mark of destruction. Form is the differentiation accumulated from the four great elements. The self-natures of the four great elements and the produced forms are not destroyed, because they are apart from both difference and non-difference. All externalists hold that the four great elements are not destroyed; the four great elements and produced forms of the three realms, within the knowable, have arising and ceasing. Apart from the four great elements and produced forms, on what do all the externalists ponder impermanence? The four great elements are unborn, because their self-nature marks are not destroyed. Apart from the primal-creation impermanence, it is not the four great elements. There are also other great elements, each with different marks. Because of their self-marks, no difference is obtainable; they are without difference. These do not create again, and the two expedient means are not made — know that this is impermanence. The impermanence of the destruction of shape and place: the four great elements and produced forms are not destroyed, but in the end are not destroyed. Mahamati! The end: when analyzed down to atoms and observed, there is destruction. The four great elements and produced forms, seen as different in shape and place, have no length or shortness obtainable; it is not the four great elements. The four great elements are not destroyed, while the destruction of shape and place appears. This falls into the school of enumeration. Form itself being impermanence: that form is itself impermanence. Then it is the impermanence of shape and place, not of the four great elements. If the four great elements were impermanent, it would not be the worldly conventional speech. If worldly speech is not of nature, it falls into the worldly theories. One sees all natures as mere speech and does not see the arising of self-marks. The impermanence of transformation: the marks of form appear differently, not the four great elements. As gold, made into ornaments, appears transformed — it is not that the nature of gold is destroyed, but that the form of the ornament is destroyed. The transformation of the other natures is likewise. These are various kinds of the externalists' deluded views of impermanence. When fire burns the four great elements, their self-marks are not burned. If each self-mark were mutually destroyed, the four great elements and produced forms should be cut off. Mahamati! In my Dharma, arising is neither permanent nor impermanent. Why? Because outward natures are indeterminate. I speak only of the subtle mind of the three realms, and do not speak of the various marks as having arising and ceasing. The four great elements in combination are differentiated; the four great elements and produced forms are, therefore, the discrimination of two things, the grasper and the grasped. Knowing the two discriminations, one is free from the two views of outward natures and non-natures, and realizes the self-nature of mind's appearances. Discrimination arises through the activity of thought, not through non-activity. Free from the discrimination of the naturelessness of mind-nature, all the dharmas of the worldly, the transmundane, and the supreme are neither permanent nor impermanent. Not realizing the self-nature of mind's appearances, one falls into the continuity of the evil views of the two extremes. All the externalists do not realize their own discriminations; this ordinary man has no foundation, for the worldly, transmundane, and supremely supreme dharmas arise from the discrimination of speech, which is not known by the foolish.'
Far from the primal creation, and from difference in shape and place,
nature and form are impermanent — the foolish delusion of the externalists.
The natures are not destroyed; the great elements dwell in their self-nature;
the externalists' thought of impermanence is sunk in various views.
Those externalists, with no [real] birth or death,
the great elements being of permanent self-nature — what then is the thought of impermanence?
All is mind-measure; with the two kinds of mind turning,
grasping and what is grasped, there is no self or what belongs to self.
Brahma is as the root of the tree, with its branches spreading everywhere;
what I speak is likewise only that mind-measure.'

Then the Bodhisattva Mahamati again said to the Buddha, 'World-Honored One! I beg you to speak of the successive continuity of the cessation concentration of all bodhisattvas, sravakas, and pratyekabuddhas. If one is skilled in the marks of the successive continuity of the cessation concentration, then I and the other bodhisattvas will never wrongly abandon the gate of the joy of cessation concentration, and will not fall into the folly of all the sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and externalists.'
Mahamati said to the Buddha, 'World-Honored One! I beg you to speak.'

The Buddha told Mahamati, 'From the sixth ground, the bodhisattva-mahasattva, together with the sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, enters the cessation concentration. The bodhisattva-mahasattva of the seventh ground, in thought after thought, is in the concentration that is apart from the self-nature marks of all natures — which is not attained by the sravakas and pratyekabuddhas. The sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, falling into conditioned activity, enter the cessation concentration of grasper and grasped; therefore the seventh ground is not the thought-by-thought concentration. Having attained the mark of no-difference of all dharmas, not the partial attainment of the various marks and natures, and realizing in concentration the marks of the good and not-good natures of all dharmas, therefore the seventh ground has no concentration of the thought of good. Mahamati! The bodhisattvas of the eighth ground, together with the sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, have the discriminations of mind, thought, and consciousness extinguished. From the first ground to the seventh ground, the bodhisattva-mahasattva observes the measure of the mind, thought, and consciousness of the three realms, is free from self and what belongs to self, cultivates by self-discrimination, and falls into the various outward marks. The foolish have two kinds of self-mind, grasper and grasped, which turn toward ignorance, and do not realize the beginningless past evils but are perfumed by false habitual propensities. Mahamati! The bodhisattva-mahasattva, sravaka, and pratyekabuddha of the eighth ground are near nirvana. The bodhisattva is upheld by the awareness of samadhi; therefore he delights in the gate of samadhi and does not enter parinirvana. If he were not so upheld, the Tathagata-ground would not be fulfilled, and he would abandon all the works for sentient beings, and the Buddha-seed would be cut off. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, reveal for him the inconceivable, measureless merits of the Tathagata. The sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, led by the joy they attain in the gate of samadhi, entertain the notion of nirvana. Mahamati! I have laid out the seven grounds: the good cultivation of the marks of mind, thought, and consciousness; the good cultivation of self and what belongs to self; taking up the non-self of persons and dharmas; the self-marks and common marks of arising and ceasing; the good mastery of the four unobstructed insights; the gate of samadhi of the power of resolute determination; the successive continuity of the grounds; the entry into the dharmas of the path. So that the bodhisattva-mahasattva does not, being unaware of the self-marks and common marks and unskilled in the seven grounds, fall into the evil paths of the externalists, I set up the succession of the grounds. Mahamati! In truth there is no arising or ceasing here, apart from the self-nature of mind's appearances. What is called the successive continuity of the grounds and the various activities of the three realms is not known by the foolish. What the foolish do not know is that I and the Buddhas speak of the successive continuity of the grounds and of the various activities of the three realms.'

Furthermore, Mahamati! The sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those of the eighth bodhisattva ground, intoxicated by the joy of the gate of cessation concentration, are unskilled in the self-nature of mind's appearances and are obstructed by the habitual propensities of self-marks and common marks. Falling into the view of taking up the Dharma of the non-self of persons and dharmas, they entertain the notion of a delusive nirvana, and do not awaken through the wisdom of quiescence. Mahamati! The bodhisattva, seeing the joy of the gate of cessation concentration, through his original vow of compassion and the accomplishment of great pity, knows to discriminate the ten inexhaustible phrases and does not entertain the notion of a delusive nirvana. Because the notion of delusive nirvana does not arise in them, they are free from the discrimination of grasper and grasped. Realizing the self-nature of mind's appearances, the discrimination of all dharmas does not arise. Not falling into mind, thought, or consciousness, or the discriminations that cling to the self-nature marks of outward things — not born from a non-Buddha-Dharma cause, but born following wisdom — they attain the Tathagata's self-realized ground. As when a person in a dream, by expedient means, crosses over the water, and having not yet crossed, awakens. Having awakened, he thinks: is it right or wrong? Neither right nor wrong. The other causes and thoughts of beginningless seeing, hearing, cognizing, and knowing, and the various habitual propensities and various shape-places, falling into the thought of existence and non-existence, are the dream-appearances of mind, thought, and consciousness. Mahamati! Thus the bodhisattva-mahasattva, in the eighth bodhisattva ground, sees discrimination arise. Advancing from the first ground to the seventh ground, seeing all dharmas as like illusions and so forth, he crosses over by expedient means the mind-discrimination of grasper and grasped; having done so, he makes the expedient means of the Buddha-Dharma, causing those who have not attained to attain. Mahamati! This is the bodhisattva's expedient means of nirvana, not yet forsaken; free from mind, thought, and consciousness, he attains the patient endurance of the unborn. Mahamati! In the first principle there is no succession or continuity; the Dharma of the quiescence of the discrimination of nothing-at-all is spoken.'
The mind-measure has nothing at all; this abode and the Buddha-ground,
the past, the future, and the present — spoken by the Buddhas of the three times.
The mind-measure is the seventh ground; nothing-at-all is the eighth;
these two grounds are named the abode; the Buddha-ground is named the supreme.
Self-realized wisdom and purity — this is my ground,
the place of sovereign supremacy, magnificently adorned with purity.
Shining like a blazing fire, its light spreading everywhere,
its flame harms not the eye, and round about it transforms the three realms.
Transforming in the three realms, sometimes transformed in former times,
proclaiming the vehicles there — all this is the Tathagata-ground.
The tenth ground becomes the first; the first becomes the eighth;
the ninth becomes the seventh; the seventh again becomes the eighth;
the second becomes the third; the fourth becomes the fifth;
the third becomes the sixth; where there is nothing at all, what succession is there?'
Then the Bodhisattva Mahamati again said to the Buddha, 'World-Honored One! Is the Tathagata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, permanent or impermanent?'

The Buddha told Mahamati, 'The Tathagata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is neither permanent nor impermanent. Both of these involve faults. The permanent has the fault of an agent-maker. The permanent, which all the externalists speak of, is a creator. Since there is nothing created, the Tathagata is not the permanent, because the fault of a permanent creator is involved. If the Tathagata were impermanent, the fault of an impermanent creator would be involved. The aggregates are what is marked; the marks are without nature; if the aggregates were destroyed, he should be cut off, yet the Tathagata is not cut off. Mahamati! All that is made is impermanent, so all things, like a jar or a garment, involve the fault of impermanence. The expedient means of the stock of the all-knowing one should be meaningless, because of being made. All that is made should be the Tathagata, because of the nature of the cause without difference. Therefore, Mahamati! The Tathagata is neither permanent nor impermanent.'

Furthermore, Mahamati! The Tathagata is not permanent like space. If he were permanent like space, then the stock of the self-realized noble wisdom would be meaningless. Mahamati! For example, space is neither permanent nor impermanent. Being free from the faults of permanence and impermanence, one and many, both and neither, permanence and impermanence, it is inexpressible. Therefore the Tathagata is not merely permanent.'

Moreover, Mahamati! If the Tathagata were unborn and eternal, he would be like a rabbit's horn or a horse's horn. Because of being unborn and eternal, the skillful means are meaningless; because of the fault of that unborn-and-eternal [notion], the Tathagata is not eternal.

Furthermore, Mahamati! There is yet another matter for knowing that the Tathagata is eternal. Why is that? Because the wisdom attained in non-interruption is eternal, therefore the Tathagata is eternal. Mahamati! Whether the Tathagata appears in the world or not, the Dharma definitively abides. Sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Tathagatas dwell uninterruptedly; they do not dwell in emptiness, nor is this known to foolish beings. Mahamati! The wisdom attained by the Tathagata is what prajna perfumes. Mahamati! The Tathagata is not perfumed by mind, thought, and consciousness, nor by those aggregates, elements, and sense-fields. Mahamati! All the triple existence is born of unreal imagination; the Tathagata is not born of unreal, false imagination. Mahamati! Because of two dharmas there is eternal and non-eternal, not the non-dual; the non-dual is quiescent, because of the non-dual unborn nature of all dharmas. Therefore the Tathagata, the Arhat, the fully-awakened One, is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Mahamati! Even when speech and discrimination arise, there is the fault of eternal and non-eternal; he who has extinguished discrimination is free of the foolish views of eternal and non-eternal; one of quiescent wisdom forever leaves eternal and non-eternal, free of the perfuming of the non-eternal and non-permanent.
The manifold objects have no meaning, giving rise to the fault of eternal and non-eternal.
Without discriminating awareness, one leaves eternal and non-eternal forever.
From the thesis they establish, there arise manifold confusions,
Contemplating one's own mind-measure, nothing can be spoken of.”

Then the Bodhisattva Mahamati again said to the Buddha: “O world-honored One! May the world-honored One further explain to me the arising and ceasing of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields. In them there is no self; who is it that arises, and who is it that ceases? The foolish, relying on arising and ceasing, are unaware of the ending of suffering and do not recognize nirvana.”
The Buddha said: “Excellent! Listen well; I will speak for you.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “The Tathagata-womb, the alaya-vijnana, is the cause of both good and evil, able to create all manner of destinies. It is like a conjurer who transforms various states, free of a self and of what belongs to a self. Because one does not realize it, and through the harmony of three conditions, it gives rise to [the phenomenal]. The non-Buddhists, unawakened, grasp at a creator. Perfumed by beginningless false evil habits, it is named the alaya-consciousness. It gives rise to the abode of ignorance and dwells with the seven consciousnesses, like the waves of the sea, constantly arising and ceasing, without interruption. Free of the fault of non-eternality and of the view of self, its self-nature is unstained and ultimately pure. The other consciousnesses arise and cease; mind, thought, and consciousness, thought after thought, have seven. Because of unreal imagination they seize on various objects and, in manifold forms and places, grasp at names and signs. Not realizing the forms that one's own mind displays, not realizing suffering and pleasure, they reach not liberation, but are bound by names and signs; craving gives birth to craving. Whether the causes or the conditions, those bases of sensation cease, and successively they no longer arise; apart from one's own mind's imagination, they know neither suffering nor pleasure. Entering the stilling of perception and feeling, the fourth dhyana, the true truth of liberation, the practitioner, conceiving it as liberation, neither abandons nor turns away, and is called the Tathagata-womb and the alaya-consciousness. The seven consciousnesses flow on and do not cease. Why is that? Because they arise through the conditions of their grasping; it is not the sphere of Sravakas and pratyekabuddhas who, not realizing non-self, take up selfhood and shared signs, and generate the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields. When one sees the Tathagata-womb, the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the selflessness of persons and dharmas, then [these] cease, and the stages unfold successively in a continuous advance. The views of the non-Buddhists cannot shake them; this is called dwelling in the immovable stage of the Bodhisattva. One attains the bliss of the three-samadhi gate, held by the awareness of samadhi; contemplating the inconceivable Dharma of the Buddha's own vows, one is not attached to the bliss of the samadhi gate or to the reality-limit, but advances toward the Noble Truth of self-realization, the path not shared by any Sravaka, pratyekabuddha, or non-Buddhist. One attains the path of the ten stages of the noble line, together with the body, wisdom, and will-born [forms], and leaves the activity of samadhi. Therefore, Mahamati! The Bodhisattva Mahasattva who seeks superior progress should purify the name of the Tathagata-womb and the alaya-consciousness. Mahamati! If there were none of the alaya-consciousness named the Tathagata-womb, there would be no arising and ceasing. Mahamati! But all the ordinary and the holy all have arising and ceasing; the practitioner's self-realized Noble Truth, in the bliss of the present Dharma, does not abandon the skillful means. Mahamati! This Tathagata-womb and alaya-consciousness is seen in the thoughts of all Sravakas and pratyekabuddhas. Though its self-nature is pure, because it is covered by the dust of the passions it still appears impure; not so with the Tathagatas. Mahamati! As for the Tathagata, his present state is like seeing an amala fruit in the palm of the hand. Mahamati! At this meaning I have established it by my spiritual power, causing the Lady Srimala and the wise-satisfied Bodhisattvas, etc., to proclaim and reveal the names of the Tathagata-womb and the alaya-consciousness, arising together with the seven consciousnesses. The Sravakas, grasping at views, see the selflessness of persons and dharmas. Therefore the Lady Srimala, by the Buddha's spiritual power, speaks of the Tathagata's state, which is not the state of Sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhists. The Tathagata-womb and alaya-consciousness is the sphere of wisdom of the Buddha alone and of others — wise, meaning-following Bodhisattvas. Therefore, you and other Bodhisattva Mahasattvas should diligently study this Tathagata-womb and alaya-consciousness, and not, having merely heard and understood, be content.”
The deeply profound Tathagata-womb, which dwells with the seven consciousnesses,
Gives rise to twofold grasping; the wise are far from it.
As an image appears in a mirror, perfumed by beginningless habits,
One who observes truly sees that all things are nothing at all.
As the foolish see the pointing finger but not the moon,
So one who grasps at names sees not my true reality.
The mind is the conjurer, the thought like the player,
The five consciousnesses its companions, and delusion the spectators.”

Then the Bodhisattva Mahamati said to the Buddha: “O world-honored One! May you explain to me supremely the five dharmas, the self-natures, the consciousnesses, and the two selflessnesses, with their distinct characteristics. I and the other Bodhisattva Mahasattvas, at every stage in successive continuity, would analyze these dharmas and enter all the Buddha-Dharmas; and to enter all the Buddha-Dharmas is to reach even the Tathagata's stage of self-realization.”
The Buddha told Mahamati: “Listen, listen! Reflect well on it.”
Mahamati said to the Buddha: “So be it; I receive your teaching.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “The discriminating characteristics of the five dharmas, self-natures, consciousnesses, and two selflessnesses are: name, appearance, imagination, right knowledge, and thusness. If a practitioner, practicing, enters the Tathagata's Noble Truth of self-realization, free of the views of extinction and constancy, of presence and absence, then the bliss of the present Dharma [and] its right concentration is present before him. Mahamati! Whoever does not realize those five dharmas, self-natures, consciousnesses, and two selflessnesses, [sees] external natures displayed by his own mind [as real]. This is the imagination of ordinary men, not of the noble sages.”
Mahamati said to the Buddha: “O world-honored One! How is it that the imagination of the foolish arises, while [it does not for] the noble sages?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “The foolish grasp at the names and appearances of conventional things, and flow along after the mind. Having flowed along, they [behold] various forms and images, falling into the views of self and what belongs to self, and longing to grasp at beautiful skandhas. Having grasped, ignorance covers them and arises attachment. From attachment, actions born of greed and hatred accumulate. From accumulation, delusion binds itself, like a silkworm making its cocoon, and falls into the sea of birth-and-death, the wilderness of the destinies, like a well-wheel being drawn. Because of folly they cannot know that the nature of the illusion, the mirage, the reflection of the moon in water, is free of self and of what belongs to self. They give rise to all unreal imaginations, apart from the sign and the signified and from arising, dwelling, and ceasing; [all these] arise from the imagination of one's own mind, not from an Iśvara, a time, atoms, or a supreme being. Foolish ordinary beings flow along after names and appearances. Mahamati! That appearance — what the eye-consciousness illuminates is called form; what the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousnesses illuminate is called sound, odor, taste, touch, and dharma. This is called appearance. Mahamati! That imagination is the setting up of all names, displaying various appearances — this and nothing else: the names elephant, horse, cart, step, man, woman, and so on. This is called imagination. Mahamati! Right knowledge is where those names and appearances are not to be obtained, like a passing guest; the consciousnesses do not arise, neither cut off nor constant, not falling into the stages of any non-Buddhist, Sravaka, or pratyekabuddha.”

Furthermore, Mahamati! The Bodhisattva Mahasattva, by this right knowledge, neither establishes names and appearances, nor does he not establish them; he abandons the two views of assertion and denial, knowing that names and appearances do not arise. This is called thusness. Mahamati! The Bodhisattva Mahasattva who abides in thusness, gaining the state of nothing-at-all, attains the Bodhisattva stage of Joy. Having attained it, he is forever free of all the evil destinies of the non-Buddhists, and abides rightly in the transcendent world-stage. The dharmas mature, and he analyzes all things as illusion and so on; the characteristic of the self-realized Dharma-stage, free of all false views and strange signs. Progressing successively to the stage of Dharma-cloud, in the intervals he enjoys the sovereign mastery of samadhi's power and spiritual powers, opening forth. Having attained the Tathagata-stage, by various transformations he illumines and reveals, maturing beings, like the moon in water. Perfectly fulfilling the ten inexhaustible phrases, he distinguishes and preaches the Dharma for beings of various understandings, and the Dharma-body is free of what mind makes. This is called what the Bodhisattva gains by entering thusness.”

Then the Bodhisattva Mahamati said to the Buddha: “O world-honored One! How does the world-honored One, for the three self-natures, enter them into the five dharmas? Does each [nature] have its own characteristic and thesis?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “The three self-natures and the eight consciousnesses and the two selflessnesses are all entered into the five dharmas. Mahamati! Those names and appearances are the nature of imagination (parikalpita). Mahamati! If, relying on that imagination, the mind and mental dharmas arise, and the names arise together with it, like the light with the sun — with various appearances each separately discriminated and held — this is called the dependent-originated nature (paratantra). Mahamati! As for right knowledge and thusness, being indestructible, they are called the perfected nature (parinispanna).”

Furthermore, Mahamati! The imagination displayed by one's own mind has eight discriminations, namely the alaya-consciousness, the thought, the manas, and the five consciousness bodies that are unreal appearances because of imagination. When the twofold grasping of self and what belongs to self is extinguished, the two selflessnesses arise. Therefore, Mahamati! The five dharmas — the self-realized Noble Truth of the Sravaka, pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Tathagata, the successive continuity of the stages — all the Buddha-Dharmas are entered therein.”

Furthermore, Mahamati! The five dharmas are: appearance, name, imagination, thusness, and right knowledge. Mahamati! As for appearance — when place, form, color-image, and so on appear, this is called appearance. If that has such an appearance, it is named 'a jar,' and this and nothing else is spoken of as the name. The setting up of all names, displaying various appearances, and the mind and mental dharmas of a jar, etc., are called imagination. Those names and appearances are ultimately unobtainable, from first to last without perception; there is no turning over among dharmas, free of unreal imagination — this is called thusness. The real, decisive, ultimate self-nature, unobtainable — that is the thus-appearance. It is the stage into which I and the Buddhas are conformably entered, and for beings we speak it fully as it is. Setting forth and displaying, we enter therein rightly awakened; neither cut off nor constant, imagination does not arise. Conformably entering the Noble Truth of self-realization, the sign not obtained by any non-Buddhist, Sravaka, or pratyekabuddha — this is called right knowledge. Mahamati! These are called the five dharmas, three self-natures, eight consciousnesses, and two selflessnesses; all the Buddha-Dharmas are entered therein. Therefore, Mahamati! You should skillfully study them for yourself and also teach others; do not follow another.”
The five dharmas and three self-natures, together with the eight consciousnesses,
And the two selflessnesses, gather all the Mahayana.
Names and appearances, false imagination, the self-natures in two aspects,
Right knowledge and thusness — these are the perfected characteristics.”

Then the Bodhisattva Mahamati again said to the Buddha: “O world-honored One! As the world-honored One has spoken, the past Buddhas, like the sands of the Ganges, and likewise the future and the present. How, O world-honored One, is this to be received — as said, or is there another meaning? May the Tathagata, in compassion, explain it.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “Do not receive it as said. The measure of the Buddhas of the three times is not like the sands of the Ganges. Why? Because they transcend the world's expectations, beyond what any comparison can compare. Because common men grasp at constancy and the non-Buddhists' delusions nourish evil views, and birth-and-death is endless, in order to make them weary of the round of birth-and-death and turn away, and diligently seek the higher advance, I speak thus for them: the Buddhas are easy to see, not like the udumbara flower, which is hard to behold; so I stop their seeking in the means. Again, at times regarding those to be converted, I say: 'The Buddha is hard to encounter, like the udumbara flower.' The udumbara flower is seen only as another's body — there is no 'already seen,' 'now seen,' or 'will be seen.' But the Tathagata is seen by all the world. It is not because I establish the self-realized state that I say the Tathagata's appearance in the world is like the udumbara flower. Mahamati! He who establishes the self-realized state transcends the world's expectations; that which the foolish common men cannot believe — the state of the self-realized Noble Truth — has no comparison; the true Tathagata transcends the appearance seen by mind, thought, and consciousness, and cannot be compared. Mahamati! Yet when I speak the parable of the Buddha like the Ganges' sands, there is no fault. Mahamati! For example, the sands of the Ganges are trodden by all fish, turtles, crocodiles, makaras, lions, elephants, horses, men, and beasts, and the sand does not think: 'These annoy me,' and give rise to imagination. Its self-nature is pure, with no defilement. The Tathagata, Arhat, fully-awakened One, whose self-realized Noble Truth is like the Ganges, whose great power and sovereign mastery are like its sands — though all non-Buddhists, with all men and beasts, annoy him, the Tathagata does not think and give rise to imagination; the Tathagata is quiescent with no thought. Because of his primal vow, to delight beings with the bliss of samadhi, he is not annoyed, just like the Ganges' sands, with no difference. Moreover, because he has cut off greed and hatred. For example, the Ganges' sands, being the self-nature of the earth, when the eon is consumed and all the earth burns, that earth-element does not abandon its self-nature, because it is born together with the fire-element. The other foolish men think the earth burns, but the earth does not burn, because of the fire's cause. So, Mahamati! The Tathagata's Dharma-body, like the Ganges' sands, is indestructible. Mahamati! For example, the Ganges' sands have no limit; the Tathagata's radiance likewise is without limit, and for the sake of maturing beings shines everywhere upon all the Buddha assemblies. Mahamati! For example, seeking other sands apart from the Ganges' sands, they are forever unobtainable. So, Mahamati! The Tathagata, Arhat, fully-awakened One, has no birth-and-death, no arising and ceasing, because the causal conditions are cut off. Mahamati! The Ganges' sands — their increase and decrease cannot be known. So, Mahamati! The Tathagata's wisdom maturing beings neither increases nor decreases, because it is not a matter of body; the bodily dharma has destruction, but the Tathagata's Dharma-body is not the bodily dharma. As when one presses the Ganges' sands, oil is not obtained — so, though all extremely suffering beings press upon the Tathagata, until beings have attained nirvana, he does not abandon the dharma-realm and the bliss of his own samadhi vow, because of great compassion. Mahamati! For example, the Ganges' sands flow with the water — it is not that there is no water. So, Mahamati! All the dharmas spoken by the Tathagata flow with nirvana; therefore I say, like the Ganges' sands. The Tathagata does not flow with the going [of things], for 'going' implies destruction. Mahamati! The first limit of birth-and-death cannot be known; not being known, how can one speak of 'going'? Mahamati! 'Going' means extinction, and the foolish do not know it.”
Mahamati said to the Buddha: “O world-honored One! If the first limit of beings' birth-and-death cannot be known, how can liberation be known?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “When the causal factors of the beginningless false, evil, delusive habits are extinguished, and one's own mind displays and knows the external meaning, the body of imagination turns and is liberated, not extinguished. Therefore [the limit] is boundless, not that there is nothing at all. For that delusion, names like 'boundless' are made. Observing within and without, free of imagination, there are no separate beings; wisdom and its field. All dharmas are entirely quiescent. Not recognizing the imagination displayed by one's own mind, therefore imagination arises; if one recognizes it, it is extinguished.”
Observing the teachers, like the sands of the Ganges,
Neither broken nor gone, and also not final,
This is the sameness, observing the Tathagatas.
Like the Ganges' sands, free of all faults,
Flowing yet constant in nature, this is the Buddha's right awakening.”
Then the Bodhisattva Mahamati again said to the Buddha: “May you explain the characteristic of the momentariness of all dharmas. O world-honored One! How are all dharmas momentary?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “All dharmas are: good, evil, and neutral; conditioned and unconditioned; worldly and transcendent; blameworthy and blameless; outflows and without outflows; received and not received. Mahamati! In brief, mind, thought, and consciousness together with the habits are the cause of the five aggregates of grasping; it is the habits of mind, thought, and consciousness that nourish the good and evil imaginations of ordinary fools. Mahamati! One who practices the bliss of samadhi and the right concentration of the present Dharma's bliss is called a noble and holy one, good and without outflows. Mahamati! Good and evil belong to the eight consciousnesses. What are the eight? The Tathagata-womb, named the alaya-consciousness; mind, thought, and consciousness; and the five consciousness bodies — not as the non-Buddhists speak. Mahamati! The five consciousness bodies are together with mind, thought, and consciousness. The characteristics of good and evil, turning and changing in mutual succession, flow on without interruption; the body is not destroyed, and they both arise and cease. Not realizing what one's own mind displays, the next moment the other consciousnesses arise; forms and characteristics are discriminated and grasped, and the mental consciousness and the five consciousnesses arise together, mutually corresponding, not resting for a moment, and this is called momentariness. Mahamati! Momentariness is called the alaya-consciousness [and] the Tathagata-womb, together with the thought-born consciousness and the momentariness of habit. The habit of the outflows is not momentary, not known by the foolish. Grasping at the doctrine of momentariness, they donot realize that all dharmas are both momentary and non-momentary, and by the view of extinction they destroy the unconditioned dharmas. Mahamati! The seven consciousnesses do not flow on, do not receive suffering and pleasure, and are not the cause of nirvana. Mahamati! The Tathagata-womb receives suffering and pleasure together with its causes, whether arising or ceasing. Drunken in the four abodes and the abode of ignorance, the foolish do not realize it and, with the view of momentariness, their imagination perfumes the mind.”

Furthermore, Mahamati! Like gold, like a vajra, like the Buddha's relics, having obtained an extraordinary nature, they are never damaged. Mahamati! If there were an uninterrupted momentariness, then the holy would not be holy; yet the holy has never been unholy. Like gold and vajra, though eons pass, when weighed it does not diminish. How is it that ordinary fools, unskilled in my hidden meaning, imagine all internal and external dharmas to be momentary?”
The Bodhisattva Mahamati again said to the Buddha: “O world-honored One! As the world-honored One has said, when the six perfections are fulfilled, one attains right awakening. What are the six?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “The perfections have three discriminations: worldly, transcendent, and supreme-transcendent. Mahamati! The worldly perfections are those of one who grasps at self and what belongs to self, grasping at both extremes, for the sake of the various places of rebirth, delighting in form, sound, odor, taste, and touch, thus fulfilling the perfection of giving (dana); likewise the precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom. They are the spiritual powers of ordinary men and the birth in the Brahma heaven. Mahamati! The transcendent perfections are those of Sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, who fall into the grasping of nirvana, so they practice the six perfections, delighting in their own nirvana's bliss. The supreme-transcendent perfections are those of one who awakens to the measure of the imagination displayed by his own mind, and because of his own twofold mind, does not give rise to imagination; in the destinies, he grasps not what is his lot, and does not grasp at the forms of his own mind. For the sake of the bliss of all beings, giving arises as the perfection of giving, with supreme skillful means; on that condition, where imagination does not arise, is the precept — the perfection of precepts (sila). That very imagination not arising, and knowing the grasping and the grasped, is patience — the perfection of patience (ksanti). Through the first, middle, and last watches, diligently applying the means, conformably practicing the means, imagination not arising — this is vigor — the perfection of vigor (virya). When imagination is entirely extinguished, not falling into the grasping of the Sravaka's nirvana — this is meditation — the perfection of meditation (dhyana). When one's own mind's imagination is without self-nature, and wisdom observes, not falling into both extremes, the former body turning to the superior and indestructible, attaining the Noble Truth of self-realization — this is wisdom — the perfection of wisdom (prajna).”
Emptiness, impermanence, momentariness — the foolish imagine them,
Like a river's lamps, a seed, and so they conceive momentariness.
Momentariness stills the turmoil; quiescence, free of what is done,
All dharmas are not born — this I call the meaning of momentariness.
When things arise they then cease; I do not tell this to the foolish,
The unbroken continuity perfumed by delusion.
Ignorance is its cause; the mind then arises from it,
Before form is born, what division is in between?
In successive order they cease; the rest of the mind arises from them,
When it does not abide in form, from what condition does it arise?
Because it arises from that, not from a true cause,
How without becoming, does one know the momentariness's ruin?
The practitioner's right concentration, the vajra and the Buddha's relics,
The palaces of the Abhasvara heaven, the world does not destroy them.
Dwelling in the right Dharma, one attains full Tathagata wisdom,
A bhikshu attains sameness — how does he see momentariness?
Like gandharva cities and illusions, forms have no momentariness,
In unreal forms, looking at them as though real.”

Then the Bodhisattva Mahamati again said to the Buddha: “O world-honored One! The world-honored One records that the Arhats attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, no different from the Bodhisattvas. If the Dharma of all beings is not nirvana, who reaches the Buddha-way? From first attaining the Buddha [state] to parinirvana, in between not a single word is spoken, nor is anything answered. The Tathagata is ever in concentration, so there is no reflecting and no investigating; the nirmita-Buddha does the Buddha's work. Why does he speak of the momentary, mutually destroying characteristic of consciousness? The vajra-bearing spirits always attend and guard him. He does not establish the first limit. He displays Mara, the Mara's work, the retribution of evil deeds, the Candra and the Sundari, and going out with an empty bowl; the obstacle of evil deeds appears. How does the Tathagata, having attained the wisdom of all seeds, not abandon the faults?”
Mahamati said to the Buddha: “Excellent, O world-honored One! So be it; I receive your teaching.”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “For the sake of the nirvana without remainder I speak, and for the sake of guiding those who practice the Bodhisattva way — in this and other worlds, practitioners of the Bodhisattva way who delight in the Sravaka vehicle's nirvana; to make them leave the Sravaka vehicle and advance to the Mahayana, the nirmita-Buddha gives them the record, not the Dharma-Buddha. Mahamati! For this reason, the Sravakas are recorded as not different from the Bodhisattvas. Mahamati! 'Not different' means that the Sravaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the Tathagata have cut off the obstacle of the passions and are liberated in a single taste; not that the obstacle of knowledge is cut off. Mahamati! The obstacle of knowledge is seeing the selflessness of dharmas, supreme and pure; the obstacle of the passions is the former habit of seeing the selflessness of persons, cutting off the seven consciousnesses, and the Dharma-obstacle's liberation, when the habit of the alaya-consciousness is extinguished, ultimately pure. Because of the primal abiding Dharma, before and after are without self-nature; because of the inexhaustible primal vows, the Tathagata, without reflection and investigation, preaches the Dharma; made thus by right knowledge, since he does not forget, he is without reflection and investigation. Because the habits of the four abodes and the abode of ignorance are cut off, and the two passions cut off, free of the two kinds of death, awakening to the selflessness of persons and dharmas, and cutting off the two obstacles. Mahamati! The seven — mind, thought, consciousness, and the consciousnesses of the eye, etc. — their momentary habit-causes being cut off, the good, outflows-gone qualities are left, and they no longer revolve. Mahamati! The Tathagata-womb is the cause of the round of birth-and-death and of nirvana, of suffering and bliss; confusing the mind of emptiness, Mahamati! — the foolish common man cannot realize it. Mahamati! He whom the vajra-bearing spirits guard is only the nirmita-Buddha, not the true Tathagata. Mahamati! The true Tathagata is free of all the measures of the sense-organs; when the measures of all common men, Sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists are entirely extinguished, he attains the bliss of the present Dharma, by the patience of the uninterrupted Dharma-wisdom — not guarded by the vajra-bearing spirits. All nirmita-Buddhas are not born of action. The emanation-Buddha is not the Buddha, yet not apart from the Buddha. For the sake of beings' actions, like the potter's wheel, he preaches the Dharma; he does not speak of the self-realized state from the stage of self-realization.”

Furthermore, Mahamati! The foolish, relying on the extinction of the seven consciousness bodies, give rise to the view of extinction. Not realizing the alaya-consciousness, they give rise to the view of permanence. From their own delusion, they do not know the first limit. When the delusion of one's own mind is extinguished, there is liberation. Because the habits of the four abodes and the abode of ignorance are cut off, all faults are cut off.”
The three vehicles are also not vehicles; the Tathagata is not worn away,
All the Buddha's teachings, spoken, leave all faults and evils.
For the sake of the uninterrupted wisdom, and the nirvana without remainder,
Guiding the inferior ones, therefore the speech is hidden.
The wisdom that the Buddhas raise is the discriminating path,
The many vehicles are not vehicles; that is not nirvana.
Desire, form, existence, and views are called the four abodes,
Arising from the mental consciousness, the consciousness-dwelling where the mind abides.
The mind and the eye-consciousness and so on, extinguished as impermanent,
Or for the view of nirvana, one speaks of the permanent dwelling.”
Then the Bodhisattva Mahamati asked in verse, saying:
Those Bodhisattvas who seek the Buddha-way,
Wine, flesh, and the onion — what of their food?
May the supreme honored One, in compassion, speak it.
What the foolish crave is foul and without name,
The tigers' and wolves' delight — how can it be eaten?
Eating gives rise to many faults; not eating is the good,
May you explain the guilt and merit of eating or not.”

Having asked thus in verse, the Bodhisattva Mahamati again said to the Buddha: “May the world-honored One, for our sakes, speak of the merit and fault of eating or not eating flesh. I and the Bodhisattvas, in the present and the future, will, for the various beings who long to eat flesh, discriminatingly preach the Dharma, making them disposed to kindness toward one another. Having obtained the kind disposition, each in his own dwelling-stage, pure and clear, will quickly attain the ultimate supreme bodhi. The Sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, having stilled their own stages, likewise will attain the supreme bodhi. The evil, false doctrines of the non-Buddhists, with their wrong views of extinction and constancy and perverted grasps, still have a rule of restraint that does not allow eating flesh. How much more the Tathagata, the world's refuge, whose right Dharma is accomplished — should he eat flesh?”

The Buddha told Mahamati: “There are innumerable causes for which one should not eat flesh; yet now I shall speak them briefly for you. All beings, from the beginning, through successive causal relations, have always been the six relatives; because of the thought of kinship, one should not eat flesh. The flesh of donkeys, mules, camels, foxes, dogs, cattle, horses, men, and beasts, because the butcher mixes and sells them, one should not eat flesh. Because they are grown from unclean elements of odor, one should not eat flesh. Beings hearing the odor all become terrified — as the candala and the domba, whom dogs hate and fear, and bark at in flocks — therefore one should not eat flesh. And because it causes the practitioner's disposition of kindness not to arise, one should not eat flesh. What the common fools crave is foul, unclean, and without good name, so one should not eat flesh. Because it causes incantations and spells not to succeed, one should not eat flesh. Because the one who kills, seeing the form, rouses consciousness and is deeply attached, one should not eat flesh. Because the eater of flesh is abandoned by the devas, one should not eat flesh. Because it makes the breath foul, one should not eat flesh. Because [it brings] many evil dreams, one should not eat flesh. Because in the empty forest the tigers and wolves smell the odor, one should not eat flesh. Because it makes food without measure, one should not eat flesh. Because it does not make the practitioner arise disgust, one should not eat flesh. I have always said: whatever one eats, one should think of it as the flesh of one's own son, and as medicine; therefore one should not eat flesh. For one to allow eating flesh is not at all right.”

Furthermore, Mahamati! In the past there was a king named Simhasudasa, who ate all kinds of flesh, and in the end came to eat human flesh; his ministers and people could not bear it, and at once rebelled and cut off his sustenance. Because the eater of flesh is thus at fault, one should not eat flesh.”

Furthermore, Mahamati! All those who kill, for the sake of wealth and profit, kill, butcher, and sell. Those foolish beings who eat flesh, with money as their net, catch that flesh. The killers, whether with wealth, with hooks, or with nets, take those beings that move in the air, in the water, and on land, and kill them in various ways, butchering and selling for gain. Mahamati! Nor is there any flesh without teaching, without seeking, without imagination. For this reason, one should not eat flesh. Mahamati! At times I have spoken of forbidding five kinds of flesh, or establishing ten kinds. Now in this sutra, all kinds, at all times, I throw aside the means and sever all [flesh]. Mahamati! The Tathagata, Arhat, fully-awakened One, has nothing to eat, much less fish and flesh — nor does he teach others [to eat]. Because of the great compassion that goes before, he regards all beings as [his] only son, therefore he does not allow eating the flesh of one's son.”
All have been kin, defiled and unclean, mixed,
Born of uncleanness, hearing the odor all are terrified.
All flesh and onion, and the leeks and garlic, etc.,
And the various wines of indulgence, the practitioner ever leaves far behind.
He also leaves sesame oil, and all the perforated beds,
Because those small creatures are in them most terrified.
Eating and drinking breed indulgence; indulgence breeds the perceptions,
From perception is born craving; therefore one should not eat.
From eating is born craving; craving makes the mind drunken,
Drunk, it grows love and desire; birth-and-death is not released.
For profit they kill beings; with wealth they net the flesh;
Both are evil deeds; at death they fall to the crying hell.
Without teaching, thought, or seeking, there is no triple-pure flesh,
It has no cause without them; therefore one should not eat.
Those practitioners, therefore, are wholly far from it,
The world-honored Ones of the ten quarters all reprove it.
Eating one another in turn, at death they fall to tigers and wolves,
Foul and loathsome, born ever in folly.
Many are born as candalas, hunters, and domba types,
Or born as the yaksini, and the flesh-eating natures,
Rakshasas and cat-owls, and so forth, born everywhere therein.
The elephant-taming and the great cloud, the Angulimalya,
And this Lankavatara-sutra — I wholly forbid the eating of flesh.
Reproved by all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Sravakas,
Having eaten, without shame, life after life always dull and dark.
First I spoke of the seen, the heard, and the doubted, and cut off all flesh,
But delusion, not realizing this, gives rise to the place of flesh-eating.
Like that fault of craving, obstructing the holy liberation,
Wine, flesh, onion, leek, and garlic, all are obstacles to the holy path.
Beings of the future world, speaking foolishly of flesh,
Say this is pure and blameless; the Buddha allows us to eat.
Eat as though taking medicine, and as [eating] the flesh of your own child,
Content, arising disgust, the practitioner walks begging alms.
One who dwells in loving-kindness, I declare, ever turns away;
With tigers, wolves, and evil beasts he ever may together stay.
If one should eat the flesh and blood, all beings then are filled with dread;
Therefore the practitioner, with loving heart, will never eat of meat.
To eat of meat is to lack compassion, and ever turn from true release,
And to go against the sacred marks that holy ones reveal—therefore one should not eat.
One is reborn among the Brahmin line, and in places of practice all,
In families of wisdom and of wealth—this comes from eating no meat.”
